records.text: Joining a world brings a private **Your people await you** dispatch. Rising again after losing your realm brings **Begin again** for your new Host. Open it from the dispatch strip or the **Notifications** drawer; the archive keeps the same text for you to revisit.

It explains the world's game day length, movement, your Host's reserves, food, the gods, travelling orders and the path to bronze. Its amounts come from the rules when that Host begins. Your Host lives on subsistence before founding, so its reserves do not drain while you search for a home. When you begin again, your standing with the gods is kept.
The dispatch is a record of that beginning; use this Codex and the current city and army views as your situation changes.

records.section: Three rules that explain almost everything
records.text: **Game days belong to the world.** The world advances one game day at a time, and every duration the game shows you counts in game days. See [[time]].

records.section: Three rules that explain almost everything
records.text: **The world runs without you.** Nobody pauses. Fields are worked, soldiers are paid and granaries fill and empty while you sleep. You do not win by being online more; you win by leaving good [[routes|standing orders]] and by reading [[coming-back|what happened while you were gone]].

records.section: Three rules that explain almost everything
records.text: **Command is never instant.** An order to an army in the field travels by Runner, a person who has to walk there. Until he arrives, the army does what it was last told. See [[runners]].

1. [[getting-in]] — joining a world.
2. [[horde]] — you start as a people on the move, not as a city.
3. [[founding]] — the one decision you cannot undo.
4. [[screen]] — what every button on the screen does.
5. [[city]] and [[citizens]] — putting your people to work.
6. [[food]] — the thing that kills young cities.
Unfamiliar words are explained in the [[glossary]].
When something seems wrong, it may be a known [[rough-edges|rough edge]] — or worth a [[report]].
You are a **Wanax**: a Bronze Age ruler of a people on the eastern shores of a great sea. Many of you share one world, and it keeps moving whether you are watching or not.

This Codex is the world's book of knowledge. Every article links onward — follow what you are curious about, or open it from the **?** on any drawer or notification to read about exactly what is in front of you.

Click your Wanax name at the top left to open **Account**. Its realm summary has five rows for your selected world: your Wanax name, founding game day, owned active cities, their total population, and your realm's Kharis.

**Since today 18:34**, or another clock time and date, marks the founding of your current life. If you have risen and started again, it follows that new life. A Host that has not founded its capital shows **Not yet founded**. The population is the population of your cities; it does not include your travelling Host. No other ruler's cities or statistics appear here.

From [[keryx]], use `keryx me`, or `keryx me --json`. The API is `GET /api/v1/worlds/{world}/me` with your Bearer token. It returns only your own realm in that world.

The same account window lets you change your password, open [[community-chat]], and sign out. To delete your account, write to the admin in the community chat.
After signing in you land on the join page, which names the world and how many Wanaxes are already in it. Press **Enter the World** and you are in — as a [[horde|Nomadic Host]], not as a city.

records.section: A world that has not begun
records.text: A new world stands still until enough Wanaxes have entered it. Until then no game day passes: nothing is produced, eaten or delivered — and no orders are taken. You can look around, read this Codex and file reports, but every order is refused with *"The world has not begun — 1 of 4 Wanaxes have arrived"* (the numbers are the world's own) until the last of them enters. This is deliberate, so that whoever arrives first does not grow on everyone else's waiting time.

records.section: A world that has not begun
records.text: The **Notifications** drawer (☍) tells you whether the world has begun and how many more Wanaxes it is waiting for. If the date in the top bar never changes, this is almost certainly why. See [[time]].
A session does not last forever. If an action answers that your session has expired, reload the page and sign in again — nothing in the world is lost.
The front page has two tabs: **Sign In** and **New Player**.

- **New Player** asks for a username and a password (twice). The button says **Claim your seat**. There is no email and no password reset, so choose something you will remember. You can *change* your password from inside the browser: click your name in the top bar to open the Account window. The command-line client has the same verb, `keryx password` — see [[keryx]].
- **Sign In** takes your username and password.

The world advances one **game day** at a time. Wherever the game tells you how long something takes — a march, a building, a letter — it counts in game days, because that is the unit your decisions are made in.

How much real time a game day takes is set per world. A test world can run faster than normal. The **date in the top bar** is the world's own calendar; the sun and moon beside it show the time in the world. **When something happens** uses your clock and date: **today 18:34**, **tomorrow 09:10**, or **Thu 09:00**; further away, a date is shown. **How long something lasts** stays in game days of the world: **food for 12 game days**, or **a 30-game-day expedition**. Arrival estimates follow the world's current pace; they can change when the world pauses or its pace changes.

records.section: The world does not wait for you
records.text: Everything keeps happening while you are away: production, eating, [[upkeep|pay]], marches, battles, the gods' moods. That is why the most useful skills in Megaron are the ones that work while you are absent — [[routes|standing orders]], well-filled [[food|food stores]], a [[stances|watch]] on the approaches — and why the [[coming-back|Notifications archive]] never throws anything away.

A new world's clock is frozen until enough Wanaxes have joined (see [[getting-in]]). You can look around while you wait, but no orders: building, recruiting, placing people, marching, founding your city, sending messengers — each is refused with *"The world has not begun"* and a count of how many Wanaxes have arrived. Give them once the world starts.

Beside a planned duration, details show about how many real hours it takes at this world’s current pace and the estimated local completion time. Dense rate tables use **per game day**. The same number of game days may take a different amount of real time in another world or after its pace changes; the live estimate uses this world’s clock.
A game day is one tick of the world; its real duration depends on the world.

- **Your Wanax name**, on the left.
- **Dispatch chips** slide in when something happens. Click one to open it. **✕ all** clears the chips — they stay in the archive.
- **Date and the sun or moon** — the world's calendar ([[time]]).
- **☍** opens the Notifications archive, with a badge for unread events ([[coming-back]]).
- **⌕** opens search (also `f` or `/`): your cities, cities you can see, your armies, received letters and rumours. Search letters by their text or Wanax names, and rumours by text, region or category. Arrow keys move; Enter jumps to a map result or opens Letters/Gossip. Letters come from your current inbox (up to 30), not a full correspondence archive; rumours come from the latest 30 items in the Gossip feed. Reopen search to refresh.
- **?** opens this Codex.

| | Drawer | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| 🏛 | **City** | One settlement: people, production, buildings, garrison — [[city]] |
| ⚔ | **War** | Forces, recruiting, armies in the field — [[units|Forces]] |
| ✉ | **Diplomacy** | Letters, trade offers, known cities and rulers — [[messengers]] |
| ⚖ | **Economy** | Goods across all cities, transfers, standing orders — [[goods]] |
| ⛩ | **Kult** | The gods — [[kharis]] |
| ✎ | **Report** | Tell the builders something is wrong — [[report]] |
Every drawer has a **?** in its header that opens its article here.

- **Left-click a hex** to look at it — the inspect panel opens on the right on a wide screen, titled by its ground. On a hex your own people work it also says how many workers are there and what they produce. A foreign city shows its owner and **Defence** says **Defended** when walls or land defenders are seen, or **No defenders seen** when both are known to be absent. **Unknown** means the defence data could not be read. You can still write a message or open **March here**.
- **Right-click a hex** to give an order there — the march menu opens ([[marching]]).
- On a touchscreen, drag with one finger to pan, tap a hex to inspect it, pinch with two fingers to zoom, and hold still briefly to open orders.
- Drag, or use WASD or the arrow keys, to pan. **+** and **−** zoom, **⌂** re-centres.

- **♫** silences all sound: the sign-in screen's opening theme, the music, the horn when troops receive a march order, the clash of a resolved battle, a short call when your forces arrive, and a soft chime for each new dispatch while you are playing.
- **⚒** toggles an activity overlay.
On mobile, windows fill the screen. Use the close button at the top right to return to the map. Opening another window closes the previous one.
The map, drawers and dispatches show your realm and let you give orders.

While the Runner is still on the road, the order shows under the unit in **War → Forces** and in `keryx army`, with the next meeting time — it disappears once he has delivered it. If the unit moves again, the meeting estimate can change; it does not promise that the order is already delivered.
The one exception is your [[horde|Nomadic Host]]: you travel with it in person, so it obeys at once.

records.section: Why this is good for you
records.text: Because orders move at walking pace, **a defender who is offline is not helpless.** An attacker has to cross ground you can see, and your answer usually has less ground to cross than his army does. Distance is the defender's ally. See [[defence]].

Sometimes a Runner arrives and the order can no longer be carried out. You get an *Order failed* notification that names the order and the reason. Look at the unit in **War → Forces** and decide again.
Recall and redirect are sent from **War → Forces**, or — for redirect — by right-clicking a new destination for a unit that is already marching. See [[marching]].

records.section: Catching up with a moving unit
records.text: A unit on the march does not wait for its orders. A Runner sent to it — to recall it, redirect it or change its [[stances|stance]] — is aimed at the point on its road where he can **catch up** with it, and the game tells you when he will. Runners are quicker than soldiers, but not endlessly: a recall or redirect that cannot catch the unit before it arrives still sends a Runner to its destination. For a newly sent land order, a missed meeting is not the end of the journey: if the unit has moved again, the Runner keeps the order and follows it along a new physical route. March, recall, redirect and stance orders take effect only when the Runner and the unit actually meet. The pending order says when its next meeting is expected and when it is following a new route. If it must wait before it can continue, the pending order says so without promising a delivery time. A Runner cannot deliver to a destroyed unit or one you no longer own.

records.section: Catching up with a moving unit
records.text: Letters to other Wanaxes travel the same way, but they are sacred and cannot be stopped: see [[messengers]].

A Runner whose road to your unit crosses open water cannot swim it — it waits in your own port for a ship — anyone's — to sail that way, the same as a letter does. See [[sea]] for how the crossing works, and what happens if the ship carrying it is lost.

**Diplomacy → Runners** (or `keryx runners`) shows every runner of yours that is still out, in groups: **waiting for a ship**, **on the way**, **aboard a ship**, **waiting for an answer**, and **on the way home**. A waiting runner says where it stands, since when, and why — and offers **Arrange passage** (one of your own free ships) or **Call back** (only when it waits in your own port). A runner **waiting for an answer** has reached the other Wanax's city and stands there until they answer — the tab says since when, and when it heads home if nobody does. An order's runner names the order it carries. Times are the clock time something happens — "today 18:34" — never a game day count.

The tab also lists other Wanaxes' runners, but only where you can know they are there: standing in one of your cities or ports, or aboard one of your ships. You see whose runner it is and where — never what it carries, and never the road it came by. Runners are sacred; a ship's captain does not read the letters. See [[messengers]] and [[sea]].

On land a Runner needs half a foot army's terrain time ([[marching]]). At an
ordinary river crossing he uses the ship's river cost; at a ford he wades.
At sea he has no separate speed: he travels with the real ship carrying him.

A runner follows a saved land route one province at a time, including the walk to a harbour and the walk after landing. It sees from each province when it reaches it, and remembers that ground even while you are away. Runners remain sacred: they cannot be intercepted.
**Command is never instant.** This is the rule that makes Megaron different from most strategy games.

When you tell a unit in the field to turn around, change course or change stance, you do not reach the unit — you send a **Runner**, a real person who must walk to it. The game gives the next meeting estimate, such as *"Runner following the unit — next meeting today 22:40."* Until then the unit keeps doing what it was last told.

It is a permanent record of everything that happened to you — there is deliberately no "clear all". Urgent events are marked. Critical food warnings and a garrison’s latest hunger warning appear first. When that city’s recovery arrives, its old hunger warning returns to its place in history. Each notification shows when it happened using your clock and date, such as **yesterday 14:05**. If its time cannot be established, it says **time unavailable**.
Click any row to open it in the **Dispatch window**. The same window opens from a dispatch chip in the top bar. It gives you:

- what happened,
- **⌖ Take me there**, which jumps the map to where it happened,
- on a letter or a trade offer, **✉ Reply** instead, which opens your letters with that Wanax (in Keryx: `keryx letters <id>`, printed under the notice),
- **? Read about this**, which opens the Codex article that explains it,
- a checkbox, *Stop these as dispatches*. Muting only silences the chip. The event is always kept in the archive. In [[keryx|Keryx]] the same setting is `keryx dispatches --mute <Kind>`, and it is shared between the two.

1. **Food** — a [[food|shortfall]] kills people every game day it lasts.
2. **Pay and bread** — [[upkeep]] warnings mean soldiers need silver or food. Soldiers share grain, fish, oil and wine with the people, but their meals are itemized separately. Produce more food or send a [[transfers|transfer]]. A notice marks when garrison hunger starts and when it ends.
3. **Foreign marches** — someone is coming, and you know roughly when. See [[defence]].
4. **Sieges and occupation** — a clock is running on a city. See [[sieges]] and [[occupation]].

A [[kharis|Kharis]] notice marks each change between Favorable, Indifferent, Suspicious and Wrathful. Check **Kult** for Kharis and the upkeep of the cult. It fades from the start; every active city and its residents count toward the cost. A warning marks a fall below 30 with negative net; below 15 punishment can fall, with or without a temple. An actual punishment protects you for seven game days; Kult shows when this protection ends. Staff and feed temples, then check the projected net.
Then look at **City → Production** for idle [[citizens]], and **Diplomacy → Correspondence** to ask a contacted Wanax about [[trade]].
Set up [[routes|standing orders]] for food and materials, keep [[food|food]] in the city’s stores, and post a [[stances|watch]] where enemies would come from.

Historical food reserve releases, food support reports and food reserve warnings are grouped at the end of Notifications. Choose **show reports** to read them; **All notifications** returns to the archive. Rumours you have heard are mixed into the same list, each marked **Rumour**.
While you were away, the world kept moving. Here is how to catch up.

- **A thousand people**, and they are the city you will found — its starting population, not soldiers. <!-- src: api/handlers/nomadic_host.go nomadicHostPopulation -->
- **Two cohorts of spearmen escort you.** They live on grain and draw no silver pay, just like settled spearmen.
- **The Host itself eats nothing.** A people on the move carries its own bread. The grain in the store is a dowry that goes into your city's stores the game day you found.
- **The Host cannot fight.** The escort can.
- **It sees two hexes** (further across open water or towards mountains) — exactly the ground a settlement would work. Wherever the Host stands, it can see the whole [[catchment]] it would get by stopping there.

**Right-click any hex** to open the order menu, pick the Host and press **March →** — or left-click a hex and use **March here →** in the inspect panel. The Host moves at 90% of Spearmen's speed and reveals the map as it goes.
Unlike everything else you will ever command, **the Host obeys instantly**: you are walking with it. See [[runners]] for what comes after.

The Host's marker, sight and founding place follow the Province it physically occupies, including during a march. Its hover and panel say **Marching**, **Waiting** (with the reason this ground cannot be settled), or **Can found here**. Click the marker's current hex to open the Host panel. Keryx `founding status` and `status` show the same position and state.

You can found on valid ground while the Host is marching. The city rises where the Host stands when you confirm, and the Host disappears. If it has moved from the place you confirmed, the order is refused; reopen its panel and read the new site before founding.

Before founding, the Host lives on subsistence and its reserves do not drain. A new Host carries **120 silver**; a Host rising after losing every city starts with **60 silver**. Its grain and silver go into your city when you settle. Your [[welcome|opening dispatch]] records what your Host carries. Choose your site for its food, resources and position.
When you have found your place: [[founding]].

You do not begin with a city. You begin as a **Nomadic Host** — a whole people on the move, standing as one token on the map. There is no separate founding screen: the map is the game from the first second.
Find it (the map centres on you) and **left-click the hex it stands on**. The inspect panel opens, headed *Nomadic Host*.

The [[horde|Host]] panel shows the terrain and four short assessments for the hex you stand on: **Feeds itself: yes/no**, **Timber: yes/no**, **Stone: yes/no**, and **Ships: yes / never — inland**. An inland metropolis can never build a harbour or ships ([[buildings]]). They use the existing forecast for known ground; unknown means the forecast is unavailable. The [[catchment]] you would claim glows on the map. Open **Details** for the full founding forecast, deposits, production, gifts, each catchment hex, and the Host’s people and supplies. It updates as you walk.
Under **Details**, the forecast gives the grain your fields would produce against what your people would eat, and one of three verdicts:

- **It feeds itself** — the fields cover the mouths with room to spare.
- **Marginal** — positive but thin. Draft one cohort and you are eating into the food stock.
- **It does not feed itself** — you are told how many game days your carried grain buys, and whether a Farm would fix it. If it says a farm will not help, there is no farmable ground in reach at all.
The gap between *marginal* and *does not feed itself* has killed more young cities than any war. See [[food]].

In **Details**, below the grain line, look for **deposits**: copper, tin, silver, cedar. A site with metal under it is worth walking extra game days for. A site with none is not a mistake — you can buy metal ([[trade]]) — but you will be buying it from someone who walked those game days. Read [[bronze]] before you decide.

Not on sea, mountain, river or semi-desert, and **not within two hexes of another settlement** — city centres stand at least **three** hexes apart. Closer than that, the game refuses and tells you how far to move. At three or more your [[catchment]] may share ground with a neighbour's; who works a shared hex is told in [[catchment]].

The Host panel follows its current physical position, including on the march. **Waiting** explains why the current ground cannot be settled; **Can found here** means the site is valid. If the Host has moved while you were confirming, reopen the panel before trying again.

Press **⚒ Found the metropolis here** at the bottom of the Host panel. Read the warning beside the button, then press **Found the metropolis** to confirm. **Keep travelling** closes the warning without founding. In exchange:

- The Host's people become your city's population.
- Everything carried — grain and silver — pours into the city. A new city starts with **no timber and no stone**: its [[catchment]] needs ground that produces these materials (or a neighbour to buy from) before the first building can rise.
- Forces standing on the hex become its garrison.
- **Demeter's gift**: found inland, with farmable ground in your catchment, and a Farm appears, free.
- **Poseidon's gift**: found on the coast and a galley is waiting in the harbour — instead of the farm. The sea feeds a harbour city; a gift is one or the other, never both.
- Your first [[citizens]] are placed on the best food land automatically, until the city feeds itself — and always at least one, so even a colony of 100 has someone in the fields. The rest stand idle, waiting for you.
Next: [[city]].

The forecast lists grain and fish production separately from the population's full food consumption. A production deficit uses up carried grain before hunger begins. Fish counts as food. Hunger begins only when daily meals are not fully covered, after stored grain, fish, oil, wine and emergency livestock have been used. A production deficit warns of future hunger once reserves run out; it does not by itself mean the population is starving.

If the known catchment has no timber or cedar to cover timber costs, the forecast warns before you found. Unknown ground may still hold wood; scout it or plan deliveries. A fully known catchment without wood needs imports for building.

Place citizens on olive groves, maquis, hills or river valleys for timber, or on cedar forest for cedar to cover timber costs, and on stone-bearing ground for stone; idle citizens produce nothing. Maquis, hills and river valleys each have one timber place before a Lumbermill is built, yielding 0.33 timber per worker per game day ([[catchment]]). The forecast says when Demeter’s farm is already included; another farm is not an extra founding gift.

On grain-bearing hills, a Farm at level 1 makes 0.85 grain per worker per game day, with room for five workers. Plain hills give 0.5 per worker. With another grain-bearing hill in reach, six food workers can feed a new city of 1,000 people; leave the rest for timber and stone. Check the forecast for your actual site.
Founding your first city — the **metropolis** — is the one decision in Megaron you cannot undo. The Host dissolves forever.
Survivors set out again as a small [[horde|Nomadic Host]]:

- **Between 400 and 800 people.** The number falls as it falls. <!-- src: api/handlers/rise.go risenHostMinGubbar/risenHostMaxGubbar -->
- **One company of spearmen** as escort, where a newcomer has two.
- **60 silver**, a fixed reserve; the spearman escort draws no silver pay. Bread for the road is the same as a newcomer carries.
- **Another shore.** Refugees do not stay where the enemy stands. The Host is set down on another landmass, or on an island, wherever there is free ground.
Until you found a city, your Host stands under the gods' protection: anyone who attacks it loses 70 kharis. See [[xenia]].
Everything you knew stays yours: your letters, the cities you have [[contact|made contact with]] and the map you have seen. Then it is [[founding]] again, as at the very start.

You leave this world for good and cannot rise in it again. **Your account remains**, and the next world is open to you. To delete the account itself, write to the admin in the [[community-chat|community chat]].
In [[keryx|Keryx]] the same two choices are `keryx rise` and `keryx leave`.
See also: [[occupation]] and [[sieges]], for how a city is lost, and [[xenia]] for the gods' order among the Wanaxes.

When your last city falls, to hunger, to a conqueror's annexation or to fire, your reign in it is over. The screen that follows tells the story of that reign, from the city's rise to its fall. Under the story you choose what comes next.

**Left-click your own city** and the City drawer opens on it. If you hold several settlements, the **‹** and **›** arrows in the header cycle between them; your capital is marked **★**.

The drawer has three tabs: **Production**, **Buildings** and **Garrison**. If your city is under siege, a red banner at the top names who holds the approaches ([[sieges]]).

## Production — the dashboard

Three sections show the essentials:

- **Population** — whole citizen groups, those free to work, and livestock. One citizen represents 100 people; fewer than 100 remaining people do not make a free worker. The exact population is under **More**.
- **Catchment & workplaces** — the placement grid, where you put people to work. See [[citizens]].
- **Food** — how many game days the city’s current grain, fish, oil and wine stocks last at current consumption, whether stocks are growing, and whether the fields can feed everyone. See [[food]].

Open **More** for people in service and the labour pool, **Devotion** ([[temples]]), **Food details** ([[food]]), **Last game day**, and **Daily history → Show recent game days**. These details and controls remain available while the main view stays short.

## Buildings

What stands, what is queued (with a **✕** to cancel), forces in training, and **Construct**. See [[buildings]].

## Garrison

The forces standing in this city. Orders to them are given from **War** ([[units|Forces]]).

**Maquis, hills and river valleys also give timber:** each hex has room for one timber worker, producing **0.33 timber per game day**. A [[buildings|Lumbermill]] adds four places, making room for five timber workers, and multiplies each worker's output by ×1.7 at level 1, ×2.4 at level 2 or ×3.1 at level 3. Olive groves remain a richer source of timber; cedar forest produces cedar, which can cover timber costs.
On the map, a city's catchment is outlined in gold when you have that city in focus: when its City drawer is open, or when you click the city itself.

- **Where you found decides what you can make.** A catchment of plains and coast feeds people; one with a mountain may hold copper or silver. The [[founding]] forecast shows you the catchment before you commit.

- **Neighbours share ground.** Cities may be founded as close as **three** hexes apart, so their catchments overlap. A hex belongs to whichever city has [[citizens]] working on it; a neighbour cannot place anyone there while you hold it.

- **A held hex can be taken.** Stand one of your own forces on it in [[stances|fortify or sentry]], then place a citizen there. The holder's citizens go home to their idle pool, their building on the hex becomes yours at the same level, and any build they had queued there is cancelled and refunded. They are told by dispatch. A unit that merely marches through takes nothing, and if the holder has a unit standing guard there too, you must defeat it first ([[battle]]).
- **They can take it back** the same way: a unit in fortify or sentry, then a citizen placed.
- **A hex you have not scouted cannot be worked.** It is listed below the grid rather than drawn.

- **An enemy on your catchment hurts.** A hostile unit in [[stances|sentry]] on one of your hexes stops that hex feeding you. Hold enough of them long enough and a city falls without a battle — see [[sieges]].
A hex shown as held by another city is already being worked by that city. Shared reach does not make its workers yours; the placement card explains whether you can take it.

A settlement lives off the land around it. That land is its **catchment**: the city's own hex plus the ring of hexes within **two** steps of it — eighteen hexes of land and water that its people can work. <!-- src: internal/hexgrid CatchmentRadius -->

The catchment is the **only** place production comes from. There is no abstract "income": every sack of grain, every log and every ingot was produced by one of your [[citizens]] standing on one of these hexes, or working in a [[buildings|building]] in the city.

Open **City → Production → Catchment & workplaces**. You get a hex diagram: the centre hex labelled **City**, ringed by your [[catchment]]. Each ring hex shows its number and how many goods it can produce.
**Click a hex** and a row appears for each good it can produce, with:

- what it makes now and what **the next citizen would add**,
- occupancy as dots — filled for placed citizens, hollow for free places,
- or simply **full** when the hex is at its limit.

Each row has **+1**, **Fill** and **−1**. *Fill* keeps adding until the hex is full or your idle people run out. If a placement is refused, the reason appears in red under the rows; the hex stays selected so you can try another good.
**Click the centre City hex** to staff [[buildings]] — same rows, same buttons.

The *next citizen would add* figure is all you need for a good decision. A citizen placed past a hex's limit produces nothing, which is why the row says **full** instead of letting you find out slowly. Every good has a limit on that hex; a relevant building adds four places and raises each worker's output.

Your first citizens are placed on the best food land when you [[founding|found]]. Afterwards, each time the population crosses another hundred, the new citizen remains **free to work** until you place it. Choose a hex or the central City hex and assign that citizen to a job. Keep enough citizens producing food as your city [[growth|grows]].
Idle citizens are wasted citizens. So are citizens producing something nobody uses — see [[surplus]].
On the map, a small marker shows the hexes where your people are at work.

Fish feeds your people just as grain does. A city living on stored food is still fed. Hunger begins only when the daily meal remains short after the [[food|feeding chain]] has been exhausted; see [[growth]].

One placeable **citizen represents 100 people**. Population counts people; City and Goods count these citizens. The food-workers estimate assumes the best grain and fish slots for the population. Moving workers may require rearranging the remaining food placements; the army draws from the same food stocks, as shown separately in the food balance.

People outside whole groups of 100 automatically produce a fraction of the best food worker’s output: 42 people give 42 hundredths. They make grain or fish, whichever their best food hex produces most of, including its building bonus. This work is invisible and takes no place from your citizens. Nearby ground supplies its grain separately. City food details show these automatic contributions beside the placed citizens needed for meals. The count uses production rather than stored food; it is an estimate for the best food slots, not a recommendation to remove particular citizens.

Temple workers use the same citizen pool as other jobs. Use `keryx staff temple +1` to assign one, `staff temple -1` to free one (with several temples, add `--god <god>`), and `roster` to see their assignments. See [[temples]].
**One citizen marker stands for one hundred people.** A city of a thousand gives you ten. Each citizen stands on **one hex, or in one building, producing one good**. That is the whole labour model.
If the available food and emergency livestock run out and the game day's need is still unmet:

You get an urgent **CivilianStarvationStarted** notification when hunger is first observed. It records the game day, city and how much of that game day's meal was missing, in food. The latest start stays above ordinary history in Notifications until that city's food supply has recovered steadily. You get **CivilianStarvationEnded** after a run of fully fed game days; the old start then returns to ordinary history. Hunger returning during that recovery window belongs to the same warning. A new spell after recovery starts a new pair of notices, rather than repeating the warning every game day.

Civilian meals and [[upkeep|soldiers’ food]] draw from the same stocks, but are served separately: a city's people may be fed while its garrison is hungry, or the other way round. Each warning clears independently. If a city leaves your rule or ceases to be active, its warning closes without claiming its people recovered.

Older **FoodShortfall** messages remain in history. The world's daily food audit still records every shortfall; new inbox messages only mark the transitions. Check **City → Food details** for the current situation and act before the city keeps shrinking.

The herd breeds itself — no herder is needed. Every ten animals give one calf every **5 game days** when the city has grain to feed it (**1 grain per calf**), and every **20 game days** on pasture alone. If the grain does not reach every calf, the fed ones come on the 5-game day beat and the rest wait for the 20-game day beat. A city can only keep so many animals: the **herd cap** is 50, and every level of a **Pen** ([[buildings]]) adds 100. **Status** and **City → Food** show it as *Herd 50 / 50*, with the next calves ("4 calves in 3 game days (4 grain)"). Each animal is worth **3 food**. Animals **above** the cap are eaten **first** at the game day's meal — fresh meat does not keep — and the four goods share whatever hunger is left. If animals are still above the cap after the meal, the pen cannot hold them and they are **lost**. A bigger Pen keeps more of them. Animals under the cap stay in the herd and are eaten only if the people would otherwise starve.

- Put more [[citizens]] on grain or fish hexes. Check the *next citizen would add* figure.
- Build or level a **Farm** ([[buildings]]) — it raises how many people a grain hex can hold.
- Bring food in from another of your cities by [[transfers|transfer]] or a [[routes|standing order]].
- Buy it ([[trade]]).
- Shrink what eats: soldiers are drafted from your people and eat like them ([[upkeep]]).

Your city has food stocks: the grain, fish, oil and wine in its [[goods|stores]]. **Food for N game days** shows those stocks at current consumption, without counting future production. **City → More → Food details** shows production, the last meal by good and army food separately. Different goods forming a real share of the meal improve [[growth|population growth]]; merely storing another food does not. Stored food buys time during a shortfall. A city under [[sieges|siege]] starves because its fields are cut off, not because it produces too little.
Growth is covered in [[growth]].

Your people eat **grain, fish, oil and wine** every game day. One unit of each supplies one unit of food. The meal is shared in proportion to what is available, including the game day’s production: a city with 100 grain and 900 fish takes one tenth of its meal as grain and nine tenths as fish. No food good is used up first. If these four cannot feed the people, livestock remains their emergency food: each animal supplies 3 food. Armies, ships and caravans use the four food goods, not livestock.

A **bay** is coastal water with land on at least four of its six sides. Rivers and fords count as land for this rule; coastal water, deep water and the Thalassa do not. A missing hex beyond the map edge does not count as land. A bay doubles each fisher’s catch; it has the same two places as other coastal water.

Deep-water fishing requires the city’s [[harbour]]. The harbour supplies deep-water places without multiplying the catch. It adds no places or production to coastal water or bays. Rivers and fords keep their own fishing places and production.
A harbour creates places, not workers. Put citizens on the deep-water hexes to use them. Higher harbour levels open more places there, while each fisher still catches 1 fish per game day.

**A storm stops the fishing.** While a [[storms|storm]] stands on a fishing hex, the fishers stay placed there but catch nothing. They fish again the game day it has moved on. **City** shows *Storm over N fishing grounds*, and `keryx city` and `keryx status` print the same line: *its fishers stay but catch nothing while it stands*.

Fish feeds your people just like grain ([[food]]). Place [[citizens]] on a fishing hex in **City**, or use `keryx place fish <hex> +1`. The available places and the next citizen’s output come from that city’s current production options.

| Water | Fishing places | Fish per fisher per game day |
|---|---|---|
| Coastal water | 2 | 1 |
| Bay | 2 | 2 |
| Deep water | 0, 1, 2 or 4 at harbour levels 0, 1, 2 or 3 | 1 |

# Shipyards and workers

**An unstaffed shipyard stands still; one worker keeps it working.**

Place a citizen in the shipyard through the City's workplace controls, or use `keryx staff shipyard +1 --province <city>`. The worker comes from the same workforce as farmers and temple workers.

With at least one worker, all shipbuilding and repair jobs run at their normal pace. Additional workers do not make them faster. The existing limits on simultaneous shipbuilding and repairs still apply.

You can pay for an order while the shipyard is unstaffed. It waits with **“waiting for shipyard workers”** and has no ready time. Removing the last worker pauses every build and repair; completed work and paid materials are kept. Staff the shipyard again to resume the remaining work and see a new ready time.

Work already under way when this rule takes effect keeps its remaining work. Workers are not assigned automatically.

See [[citizens|Citizens and placement]], [[units|Soldiers and ships]] and [[sea|The Thalassa]].

A harbour stands in the city and opens fishing places on **every deep-water hex in its [[catchment]]**. Build it through **City → Buildings → Construct**, or `keryx build --type harbour`. The city must meet the coast rule described in [[buildings]].

| Harbour level | Fishing places on each deep-water hex |
|---|---|
| No harbour | 0 |
| Level 1 | 1 |
| Level 2 | 2 |
| Level 3 | 4 |

Each deep-water fisher catches **1 fish per game day**, at every harbour level. The harbour has no fishing multiplier and adds no coastal places. Coastal water always has two places producing 1 fish per fisher per game day; a bay has two places producing 2 each. See [[fishing]] for the bay rule. Rivers and fords receive no harbour bonus.

The harbour has no city workplaces to staff. Place your [[citizens]] on the deep-water hexes themselves. Its role in sea trade is separate from fishing. A Shipyard is a separate building for building and repairing [[sea|ships]].

- **Variety.** Any one of the four food goods feeds people. Growth gains 10% per extra kind that forms a real share of the food eaten that game day, up to the existing variety ceiling: two substantial kinds give a 1.1 multiplier and four give 1.3. Livestock counts only if eaten as a real share of emergency food. A good merely sitting in store, or eaten only in crumbs, gives no variety bonus.

- **Size.** The city's walls set its ceiling: 2 000 people with no wall, then 5 000, 10 000 and 20 000 for a Palisade, Stone Wall and Bronze Wall ([[buildings]]). Growth runs at its full rate right up to the ceiling and then stops; a city at its ceiling never shrinks because of it. The city screen says "Walls hold N", and `keryx status` says it too.

In short: a city grows only while it makes more food than it eats; it holds steady when it does not; and it shrinks when it goes hungry. The city screen and `keryx status` say which of the three it is, and the food net behind it, for example "not growing: food net -1.7 per game day (needs more than 0)".
More people eat more, so a growing city eats into its own surplus until the balance reaches zero and growth stops — unless you put the new citizens to work on food.
Each time the population crosses another hundred, a new [[citizens|citizen]] becomes **free to work**. Choose its job yourself.
More people means more workers, more recruits and more mouths. See [[food]].

Under **Citizens**, the City screen shows ten solid steps toward your next
citizen and the exact progress out of 100 people. For example, **64 / 100** means
36 more people are needed for the next citizen you can place. The estimated wait
uses the city's current growth, including food variety and the room inside its
walls. Game days appear with a real-time estimate from your world's clock;
when one game day or less remains, it says **next game day**.

A city grows when it has a **surplus of food** — when it produces more food each game day than its people eat. Growing costs no food: the surplus stays in the same city grain, fish, oil and wine stocks that feed your people.

- **Surplus, not store.** What counts is the daily balance — grain, fish, oil and wine produced, minus what the people eat — shown as the food *net* on the city. A positive net grows the city; zero or below holds it steady, even with full stores.
- **Surplus size.** A bigger surplus fills your stores faster; it does not itself raise the growth rate.

| **Olive Press** | Refines a press-worker's oil from the settlement's groves. Works inside the city. |

| Building | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Pen** | Raises the herd cap by 100 per level (50 without one). Animals above the cap are eaten, then lost ([[food]]). Works inside the city. |

|---|---|
| **Market** | Enables trade offers and updates market price snapshots. Has no workplaces and needs no workers. |

| Building | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Temple** | Dedicated to one god: opens that god's prayers, and its workers keep your kharis. A city can hold one temple per god. More important than it looks — see [[temples]]. |

| Building | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Granary** | A city stores 2 000 of each food — grain, fish, oil and wine, not the herd. Granary level 1 to 3 raises that to 4 000, 10 000 and 20 000. A wall of level N needs a Granary of level N. Works inside the city. |

| Building | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Wall** | Palisade, then Stone Wall, then Bronze Wall. Absorbs damage in [[battle]], and **the walls set how many people the city holds** (see below). |

**The wall is the ceiling.** A city with no wall holds 2 000 people, a Palisade 5 000, a Stone Wall 10 000, a Bronze Wall 20 000. A city at its ceiling loses no one; it simply stops growing until you raise the wall. Each wall needs a Granary of the same level first — Construct shows the next wall greyed out with "needs a Granary of level 2" until you have it. See [[growth]].

**The coast rule.** A city can build a Harbour or a Shipyard only if its own hex borders the sea or a river; an inland city never can, so to reach the sea you must found a coastal colony ([[colonies]]). The [[founding]] forecast tells you which kind of site you are looking at.

**Farm, Mine, Lumbermill and Stone Quarry stand on a hex, not in the city.** When you build one of these four, you choose which hex in your [[catchment]] it goes on, and it only ever helps that one hex. You may build more than one of the same kind — two Farms on two different grain hexes each raise their own hex's cap, independently. A Mine's hex decides what it produces: build it on a copper, tin or silver deposit and it works that deposit; there is no separate building for silver.

**One building per hex.** A hex that already has one of these four — yours, or a neighbouring city's on a hex you share — cannot take another. Building the same kind again on its own hex raises its level.

Every other building, including **Harbour**, stands in the city itself. Harbour is the one exception worth naming: though it stands in the city (and needs the city's own hex to border the sea), its fishing effect reaches every deep-sea hex in your catchment at once. Harbour levels 1, 2 and 3 open 1, 2 and 4 places per deep-water hex; each fisher catches 1 fish per game day. It gives no fishing multiplier or extra coastal places. See [[fishing]] and [[harbour]].

A farm, mine, lumbermill or stonequarry makes **space for four more workers** on its hex. Each of these buildings multiplies the hex's own **production** per worker: ×1.7 at level 1, ×2.4 at level 2, ×3.1 at level 3. Silver can only be mined with a mine — without one a silver deposit gives nothing. Olive press, winery and foundry work inside the city as before.
Buildings level up to three. **A higher level makes every worker on the hex produce more** — see the rule above.

A temple is built for a god: Construct lists one row per god (`keryx build --type temple --god potnia`), and building that god's temple again raises it. Building the same building again raises it by one level; for a hex building, choose the same hex. **Levels 2 and 3 of a Harbour, Shipyard or Temple** also need **cedar**, which is scarce and often only available by [[trade]].

A building costs what it is made of: **timber** for the Farm, Market, Stable, Harbour, Shipyard and Palisade; **stone** for the Stone Quarry, Mine, Barracks, Temple and Stone Wall. The prices are shown live in Construct. If you are short of timber, your **cedar** pays the difference one for one — in buildings, ships and chariots alike.

Production workplaces need people assigned to them. The market has no workplaces and needs no workers; former market workers are free to assign elsewhere, with no population lost. Staff a workplace from the centre **City** hex of the placement grid ([[citizens]]).
If cancelling a queued build is refused, the reason appears in the Buildings tab.

The construction queue has a fixed limit, shown in `keryx build --queue`; population and building upgrades do not add slots. Finish or cancel a queued building before starting another when it is full. Hex buildings use `place`, not `staff`: for a lumbermill use `keryx place timber <hex> +2` (cedar on a cedar hex). `build --hex` accepts coordinates such as `3,-1` or the City ordinal `6`/`#6`.

A finished building can be torn down so its hex or slot is free for something else. In the Buildings tab press **Demolish** beside the building and confirm; with keryx, `keryx demolish --hex 3,-1` for a hex building or `keryx demolish --type market` for a city one. Only your own city's buildings can be demolished.

The place is free at once — the new building then takes its normal time to build ([[catchment]] has the one-building-per-hex rule). **Nothing is refunded**, and anyone working in the building or on the places it made is lifted off and goes idle; they are not lost, and you can place them again ([[citizens]]). A hex keeps its base places, so a demolished farm's field still holds its first workers. A silver deposit gives nothing without its mine, so everyone mining it goes idle.
A temple also costs **10 kharis per level**, down to 1. The confirmation shows the actual loss and any lowered ceiling; existing standing is not cut to the new ceiling. See [[temple-demolition]].
Something still under construction is not demolished but cancelled, with its cost refunded: the ✕ in the Build queue, or `keryx cancel-build`.

`keryx build --list [city]` and Construct show the current level and the cost of the next level. Without a city name, Keryx uses your capital. Each hex building has its own level and upgrade price. A refusal names the building and the level it would reach.

Construction dispatches name the building, its city and the exact hex for a field building. **Staff Lumbermill** (or the named workplace) opens that city's Production grid with the completed site selected, so you can place a worker there. Buildings without a workplace offer **Show city** instead. The build queue repeats the city and field hex beside its completion time; Keryx shows the same place with `build --queue`.
Buildings provide workplaces, defences and the facilities needed for recruitment and trade.

Open **City → Buildings**. The tab shows what is **built** (and its level), the **build queue** (with an ETA and a **✕** to cancel), **training** (forces in progress) and **Construct**. Choose from the Construct list — each entry names the building and its cost — and press **+ Build**. A notification tells you when it is done.

| **Farm** | Stands on a grain hex you choose and works that field. |

| Building | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Harbour** | Opens deep-water fishing places and enables sea trade ([[harbour]]). Stands in the city — see below. |

| Good | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Timber, stone** | The material of nearly every [[buildings|building]]. Timber comes from olive groves, maquis, hills and river valleys in your [[catchment]]. Early on, timber is almost always your bottleneck. |

| Good | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Cedar** | Found only where there is a deposit, but a cedar forest yields far more wood than an olive grove. Levels your best buildings; builds war galleys. **Cedar stands in for timber:** whatever a cost needs in timber and you lack, your cedar covers one for one. |

| Good | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Copper, tin** | The two halves of bronze — never found together ([[bronze]]). |

|---|---|
| **Bronze** | Bronze Guard, chariots, war galleys, the best walls. |

| Good | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Silver** | The currency, and the only thing that pays soldiers ([[silver]]). |

|---|---|

- **Goods** — stock, production and use of each good, city by city. The settlements table compares people, food produced minus food eaten, food game days and shortage status; select a city to close Economy and open its City drawer. Goods piling up with nothing using them are marked — see [[surplus]].
- **Transfer** — move goods between your own cities ([[transfers]]).
- **Routes & cargo** — [[routes|standing orders]] that move goods for you while you are away.
To learn what another city needs or can spare, ask its Wanax in a [[messengers|letter]] through **Diplomacy → Correspondence**, then agree a [[trade|trade offer]].

The gods weigh goods differently: bronze can count for far more than grain. **Kult**, at the temple, and `keryx rite --list` show their current reckoning before each god's preferences. What the world can spare and what the god favours both matter ([[rites]]). Wanaxes agree their own trade prices.

Production per game day is output before meals and other uses. Food net combines grain, fish, oil and wine production minus population demand. The city has one stock of each good; food coverage counts these four goods together. Shortfall waiting estimates assume current production continues, before other use.

Food for people combines the four food goods minus the population’s meal. **Food after army** subtracts the food supplied by this city to its supported troops as well. The army shares grain, fish, oil and wine in the same proportions; its silver pay is shown separately. Population growth still uses the population-only food balance.

Each good has its own storage capacity in each city. A city stores **2 000 of each food** — grain, fish, oil and wine — and a [[buildings|Granary]] raises that to 4 000, 10 000 and 20 000. The herd has its own pens. A city that already held more food when this ceiling came in keeps it and can eat it, but it never fills back above the ceiling. **StorageCapacityWarning** is an advance dispatch when the server forecasts a stock nearing its cap. Keryx status and the City drawer show the good, stored amount, capacity and **full in N game days**. The estimate uses the current net rate and deliveries on the way; it is a forecast, so changing production or orders can change it.
The forecast counts your own transports and accepted trade deliveries that you know about. An unsolicited gift from another Wanax is known only when it arrives, so it is not included beforehand.
Send goods away by [[transfers|transfer]] or use them in [[trade]]. Warehouse construction and storage-pool expansion are not available yet.

A **StorageOverflow** notification means goods have already been lost because storage was full. It records the city, good, quantity lost and the source, such as production, a delivery, returned provisions or a refund. It does not mean the entire shipment was lost: only the reported excess failed to fit. Production into a store that stays full is lost every game day; you are told when it starts, not every game day it goes on. If the forecast clears and the city later approaches capacity again, a new warning can be sent.
Everything your cities make, eat and trade is a **good**. The **Economy (⚖)** drawer shows your goods across every settlement, in three tabs: **Goods**, **Transfer** and **Routes & cargo**.

| Good | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Grain, fish, oil, wine** | Equal food goods, eaten in proportion to availability ([[food]]). Oil and wine also serve as offerings for [[rites|prayers]]. |

| Good | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Livestock** | Breeds itself in the pen (a calf per ten animals, fed with grain). Each animal is 3 food; kept as emergency food for the people when the four food goods do not cover their meal ([[food]]). |

**Silver is the currency and pays your professional forces.** Bronze Guard, chariots and War Galleys need it; spearmen, Galleys and Emporoi need no silver to recruit or maintain.

Professionals draw pay every game day. A Wanax who runs dry risks their desertion — see [[upkeep]].

## Where silver comes from

- **Out of the ground.** A silver deposit in your [[catchment]] and a **Mine** built on that deposit hex ([[buildings]]) — the same building that works a copper or tin hex; the hex decides what it produces.
- **Out of someone else's ground, through [[trade]].** Most Wanaxes will not have a deposit. That is the point: silver is why the map has merchants on it.

Silver is kept with your other goods — the **Economy → Goods** tab shows your balance ([[goods]]).

Founding moves only the silver your Host still carries into the city: a new Host begins with **120 silver**, inland or coastal. Founding adds no extra silver. A Host rising after losing every city carries its remaining refugee purse. A colony carries existing silver from its mother city, rather than receiving new currency.

Incense is found only on marked hexes of dry scrub (maquis) and semi-desert — the ground that gives almost nothing else. A marked hex shows a small amber drop on the map and the word **Incense** in its inspect panel. [[rites|Potnia's Vision]] can mark an incense source you neither see nor remember; it creates memory, never living eyes. `keryx cities` includes incense among the deposits of known cities. A deposit in your [[catchment]] needs no building: **two citizens** placed on the hex ([[citizens]]) gather it. There are about ten such places in a world of the usual size, scattered over both halves of the map and more of them in the east. Most Wanaxes will have none, which is why it is carried and traded ([[trade]]).

records.section: What it does at the altar
records.text: Any good can be offered, and wine and oil are offerings too ([[rites]]) — wine is also food, so a hungry city should keep it. For everyday prayers, incense can help meet the offering requirement, but more offering never improves the answer. For older prayers with uncertain answers, **a gift made mostly of incense can please the gods further than any other gift**: it raises the limit on what a larger offering can achieve. It never replaces your standing with the gods ([[kharis]]) — a god who does not hear you is not bought — but it is the best use of what you carry. Each god's taste is shown in the Offer row and in `keryx rite --list`; the gods of sight and omens love it most.

Bronze Age temples burned resin, not one perfume. Around the east of the Mediterranean the common kind was the sap of the terebinth tree (*Pistacia*), gathered on the dry hills of Kna'an and Cyprus and shipped in jars. The wreck at Uluburun, sunk off the south coast of Anatolia at the end of the thirteenth century before our era, carried about a hundred and fifty such jars among its copper and tin. Amphorae from Kna'an turn up in Egypt with traces of the same resin. The rarer frankincense and myrrh came to Egypt from Punt, far down the Red Sea, in small and precious loads; labdanum, scraped from the rock-rose shrubs of Crete, was the Minoan smell. Here they are all one good, **Incense**.

**Incense is the smoke the gods like best, and it grows in very few places.** It is a rare religious good: no building makes it, no recipe needs it, and nothing in your city fails without it. What it does is make an offering count for more.

Storage is effectively unlimited, but **surplus is not free.**

The **Economy → Goods** tab marks goods that are piling up with nothing using them. The waste is not shelf space. It is the [[citizens]] standing on that hex, producing something nobody needs, when they could be growing food, cutting timber or mining metal.

The fix is always the same: **move them.** Take them off the hex that overproduces and put them where the *next citizen would add* the most that you actually use. Or sell the surplus to someone who wants it ([[trade]] — ask a contacted Wanax what they need in a [[messengers|letter]]).

This is the most valuable habit in Megaron, and the one most players never build.

The goods leave your stock when sent. They travel in a physical caravan, or aboard a real free ship from your port when a sea route is used. Cargo can be intercepted. A ship remains bound until its empty voyage home finishes. A gift carries the same risk as any other cargo: on land only raiders, at sea also [[sea|storms]].

A ship damaged in interception keeps the existing [[transfers|naval interception outcome]]: half of each good is lost, half sails home. The gift notice separates the exact quantities **lost** and **sent home**. This is a physical damaged return, not an immediate refund; that voyage can itself be intercepted.
The city receives only what fits in its store. Anything that does not fit is lost. **GiftDeliveredV2** or **GiftLostV2** tells you the exact quantities received and lost. There is no return of goods.

If the city changes hands during the journey, its **new owner receives the gift**. The sender, intended recipient and actual recipient are notified. If the city has fallen or has no owner, the gift is lost.

A gift appears as a row among the letters in **Diplomacy → Threads**. The sender can see its departure; the recipient sees the outcome when delivery is resolved. It creates no trade offer and asks for nothing in return. Notifications and Keryx show the same delivery outcome.
To send goods between your own cities, use an [[transfers|internal transfer]].
The live cargo meter uses the same limits as an internal transfer: **Galley 20 / Emporos 120 goods**, one place per good of any kind. Several goods share one voyage.

A **gift or tribute** sends goods or silver to another Wanax's city, with nothing requested in return. It needs no acceptance. The city must have a known location on your map, through sight, exploration or completed contact. A rumour alone is not enough.

Open **Economy → Transfer**. Choose your sending city, a destination marked with its Wanax's name **(gift)**, one or more goods and their quantities, then **Send →**. In Keryx, use `keryx transfer --good silver --qty 20 --dest CityName`; use the settlement ID if two cities share a name. Your own cities remain [[transfers|internal transfers]].

A caravan is people and pack animals walking across the map. Others can see it on the road, but not what it carries — the cargo is a secret until someone takes it. **It can be intercepted and seized** — yours by others, theirs by you. A hostile unit on watch ([[stances|sentry]]) near the road will stop a caravan that passes. Only [[messengers]] are safe. When a land caravan is seized, both sides are told where, and exactly what cargo changed hands; the seized goods go to the raider's capital.
An internal transfer carries exactly the same risk as a trade or a gift: on land only raiders, at sea also [[sea|storms]]. Whose goods they are never changes the risk.
To move goods regularly without being there, use a [[routes|standing order]].

When both ends are coastal or harboured and a sea lane connects them, a transfer sails instead of walking — **if you have a free Galley or Emporos waiting in the sending port** ([[sea]]). No free hull there, and no land road either, and the transfer is refused with the reason why; build one at a Shipyard, or wait for one to come home.

records.text: The ship is bound to the round trip: it cannot be given any other order until it has sailed back and unloaded, empty, at its own port. What it can carry is limited by the hull's own capacity — a shipment above the limit is refused before any goods leave your stock. **One good takes one cargo place**, whether grain, stone or silver: **Galley 20, Emporos 120 goods of any kind**. The form shows the ready hull and a live **Cargo used / capacity** meter; an overload tells you how much to remove. Land caravans have no cargo limit.
A laden ship caught at sea does not always lose the same way a caravan does. One of three things happens, and you are told which:

- **Captured** — the raider takes the cargo *and* the ship. It sails off under a new flag.
- **Damaged** — half of every good is lost overboard in the fight; the ship limps home with the rest.
- **Sunk** — the cargo and the ship are both gone.
Sending to another Wanax is a [[gifts|gift or tribute]], with nothing requested in return.

Cargo follows a real route around impassable ground. Its path and the terrain costs
are fixed when each leg departs. Caravan time is **1.5 times the march time on that
same path**, rounded once to the nearest whole game day, with at least one game day per leg.
The return leg is priced separately because it enters different terrain. Cargo
quantity limits a ship's hold; it does not change journey speed.

Without a traversable road or an eligible ship on a sea lane, a shipment is refused
before goods are taken. A standing route pauses and explains the obstacle. The
arrival time shown in your cargo list is the scheduled delivery; delays or
interception can prevent that delivery.

In Keryx, `transfer` sends from your **selected city**, which may be a colony.
Check it with `keryx status`, or choose the sending city explicitly:
`keryx transfer --from Knossos --dest Mallia --good grain --qty 50`.
The sending city cannot also be the destination. A rejected self-transfer sends
nothing; use `--from` to choose the other city you meant to send from.

A coastal city can load or receive through any adjacent navigable water hex. The sea route compares those approaches and chooses the fastest reachable one; it does not fix the port to an arbitrary side of the city. Journeys already at sea keep their saved route.

Choose several goods in the same form to send them together in **one shipment**:
one caravan or one ship, one arrival, one shared fate if intercepted or sunk.
Keryx accepts paired flags: `keryx transfer --dest Mallia --good grain --qty 12 --good timber --qty 8`.
Keryx shows the same cargo total and hull capacity before dispatch.

Economy → Transfer compares **Land** and **Sea** before you send a transfer or gift. Both show the journey in game days and real time, its arrival estimate, risk and requirements. An unavailable alternative explains why: a missing connected path, no departure/arrival coast or harbour, or no free ship with cargo space. Times assume departure now; an accepted agreement or standing route departs later and checks again. A preview reserves nothing.

Land cargo can be intercepted. Sea cargo can be intercepted and the ship can meet storms; the same risks apply to your own goods, gifts, trade and standing routes. Sea needs your available Galley or Emporos at departure, enough cargo space and the existing voyage provisions.

Your selection is saved. An explicitly chosen land route never turns into a sea voyage, or vice versa, when conditions change. A standing route waits or pauses according to its existing rules if it cannot use the chosen mode. Older orders without a selection keep automatic routing.

Keryx: `transfer --by land --good grain --qty 50 --dest Petras`, or `--by sea`. The same flag works with `trade-offer` and `route`. Omit it for the existing automatic choice; the preview lists alternatives. For trade, the agreed choice covers the physical goods and payment legs, not the runner carrying the offer.
A **transfer** moves goods between two of your *own* settlements. No consent, no negotiation — simpler than [[trade]] with a stranger.

Open **Economy → Transfer**, choose *From*, *To*, the goods and their quantities, and press **Send →**. Below, **Your cargo in transit** lists everything on the road — which city it left, which city it is bound for, and its arrival time. A notification tells you when it is delivered.

- **Keep at destination** — choose a good and the stock to keep there, for example two hundred grain and fifty fish. Use **Add a good** for another row and **Remove** to drop a row. The caravan keeps those goods topped up to that level at the destination.
- **Bring home** — choose a good and the stock to leave at the destination, for example twenty stone. Zero means bring home everything available. Leave the rows empty for no return cargo. On the way back it brings home anything above that floor.

Press **Create route**. Existing routes are listed below with **Pause**, **Resume** and **Delete**. Each route shows **Keep at destination** (the target stock) and **Bring home above** (the stock left there before loading return cargo), including a zero floor. **Return cargo: none** means no goods are configured for the homeward leg. These are route settings; the cargo in each trip depends on available surplus and capacity. `keryx routes` shows the same settings. A route pauses itself when it cannot run — when there is no surplus to send, or no spare citizen to crew the caravan — and the list says why. You are told each time a route sends a caravan, and when it pauses.

- Keeping a young [[colonies|colony]] fed until its own fields carry it.
- Supplying a city that has a mine but no farmland.
- Pulling timber and stone to where you build.
Route caravans are [[transfers|cargo]] like any other, and can be raided on the road.

A route between two coastal or harboured settlements with a sea lane between them sails instead of walking — if you have a free Galley or Emporos in the sending port ([[sea]]). That ship is then **locked to the route for as long as it runs**, including the time it spends docked between trips: it cannot be sent anywhere else, loaded, or repaired until the route is paused or deleted. No free hull, and no land road either, pauses the route with the same reason a shortfall would. The ship's hold limits both legs: out, it carries what fits; home, it brings back what fits above your floors, and the rest waits at the destination for the next trip.

**Economy → Routes & cargo** shows the ship or caravan travelling on each
standing route, with its cargo and arrival. Other shipments are listed
separately. Both land and sea cargo live here; **War → Marches** is for the
forces you order to move. A route's ship remains in **War → Forces → Ships**,
with its route named on the card.

Choose **Land** or **Sea** in Routes & cargo before creating a route; Keryx uses `route --by land` or `route --by sea`. The choice is saved for subsequent departures. The comparison explains travel time, risk and unavailable alternatives; see [[transfers|land or sea]].
A **standing order** is a caravan route that runs by itself. For a game that runs while you sleep, the **Economy → Routes & cargo** tab may be the most important screen you have.

records.text: Under **New standing order**, set *From*, *To*, and which end supplies the caravan's crew. Then:
In a **Diplomacy → Correspondence** conversation (start one with **Known → Write**), expand **+ Attach trade offer** and choose:

- **Buy** — the good you want, the quantity, and the silver you offer. Your silver is held in escrow.
- **Sell** — the good you offer, the quantity, and the silver you want. Your goods are held in escrow.
Then **Dispatch →**. The offer walks with the [[messengers|messenger]], so it takes game days to arrive.

An incoming offer appears in the conversation, for example *"Wants 40 tin · Offers 200 silver"*, with **Accept ✓** and **Decline ✗**. Your own pending offers carry **Cancel offer ✗** — withdraw it and your escrow comes back. If nobody answers before it expires, the escrow comes back too. Nothing is ever lost to silence.

The runner who carried your offer waits at the other city only while the offer is open: once it is accepted, declined or cancelled, the runner turns for home that same game day. **You learn the answer when the runner is home** — the news travels with the runner, never ahead of it. A declined offer's escrow travels with the runner too: your goods or silver are back in your stores the game day the runner is home. If the runner is lost at sea on the way, the escrow comes back at once. If nobody answers, you are told when the offer expires.

An accepted trade is carried along its agreed land or sea route. It arrives as a *Trade delivered* notification. On land nothing is lost by chance; like any [[transfers|cargo]] it can be raided. At sea every ship risks [[sea|storms]].
### When it goes by sea

If both cities are coastal or harboured and a sea lane connects them, the trade sails instead of walking — carried by **your own** ship, whichever of you *sent* the offer. It makes the whole round trip: out with your half of the deal when the other side accepts, home again with their half. The other side's ships are never touched.

If your only ship is taken by something else between sending and the other side's answer, their **Accept** fails and tells them so — your offer simply stays open until it expires or a ship frees up. A shipment too heavy for the ship's hold is refused the same way, naming the capacity.

The ship is not free for anything else until it is home — outbound and return both count, same [[transfers|three fates]] (captured, damaged, sunk) as any other cargo at sea. A **Damaged** outcome on the way home still gets half the cargo back to you, never to the other side.

Ask the Wanax of a [[contact|contacted]] city what they need or can spare. Write a [[messengers|letter]] in **Diplomacy → Correspondence** (start one with **Known → Write**), then negotiate in the reply before attaching a trade offer.
What is most worth trading? [[silver]], and the half of [[bronze]] you do not have.

are fixed when each leg departs. Caravan time is **1.5 times the march time on that
same path**, rounded once to the nearest whole game day, with at least one game day per leg.
The return leg is priced separately because it enters different terrain. The number
of goods limits a ship's hold; it does not change journey speed.

Without a traversable road or an eligible ship on a sea lane, a shipment is refused
before goods are taken. A standing route pauses and explains the obstacle. The
arrival game day shown in your cargo list is the scheduled delivery; delays or
interception can prevent that delivery.
The seller receives the full agreed silver payment when it arrives. Temples take no share of religious-goods sales.

Cargo follows its planned road or sea route one province at a time. The map and `keryx cargo` show its current province and arrival time. A province is reached only after its share of the full journey; the final province is reached at the announced arrival time.

Attach a trade offer in Letters and choose **Land** or **Sea** for the goods and payment. The runner still follows its own physical route. The choice stays with the agreement and is checked again on acceptance; Keryx uses `trade-offer --by land` or `--by sea`. See [[transfers|route requirements and risks]].

**A trade offer travels attached to a letter.** There is no market screen and no public listings. You write to a specific city and pin an offer to the message — so you can only trade with cities you have [[contact|contacted]].
The **Market** needs no workers. It has no staffing places; trade does not depend on assigning citizens to it.
Every settlement, every unit standing on the map and every messenger on the road is an eye. A Runner or messenger reveals the ground on the way out *and* on the way home.

| Eye | Sees |
|---|---|
| Settlement | 3 hexes |
| Land unit, or the Nomadic Host | 2 hexes |
| Ship | 1 hex of land — a ship is blind inland, but sees the shoreline across the water it sees |
| Anyone, looking at a mountain | 2 hexes further — mountains are landmarks |
| Anyone standing at open water | 4 hexes of sea — in a straight line across open water only |

The open horizon belongs to whoever stands at the water, and it reaches only across open water in a straight line. A coastal city or a ship reads the sea out to four hexes, but only where nothing but sea lies between it and the hex it looks at: an island, a headland or a strip of shore in the way blocks the view beyond it. An army on the beach does not see a lake behind it over the hills, and an army two hexes inland does not see the sea at all beyond its ordinary two hexes. A river between banks is not the sea and opens no horizon. **A ship also sees the shore:** every coast hex that borders water on its horizon shows, so sailing along a coast maps the coastline — but not the land behind it. <!-- src: server/internal/province/hex.go SetSeaHorizons -->

The map shows **colour for live sight, grayscale for remembered ground, and black for places never seen**. Remembered ground keeps its terrain details, frozen as you last saw it. It can be wrong, and it will not tell you so.
**Foreign forces are drawn only on ground you can see live**, never on remembered ground. They are drawn with a blinking outline.

Your marching armies, ships, Runners and caravans always show their **remaining route ahead**, beginning where the actor is now. The line shrinks as they travel; nothing is drawn behind them. Solid lines mark armies, long dashes mark ships, dots mark Runners, and mixed long/short dashes mark caravans. The line shows only ground you can see live.

A foreign actor shows only a **compass arrow at its current live position**. It tells you which way the actor goes now, never its destination or full route. Your lines are azure; foreign arrows use the foreign unit's muted accent. Line patterns and arrow shapes carry meaning alongside colour. An agreed trade caravan coming to you shows its remaining route too, in the foreign accent. Its known cargo and arrival remain in the trade details. Gifts are not agreed deliveries and show only an arrow. A Runner coming to you from another Wanax also shows only an arrow. Waiting or sealed Runners have no forward route, and a Runner aboard follows the real carrier. Runners remain sacred and cannot be attacked.

You cannot **march** an army into land none of your people has ever seen — but you can **explore** it. Right-click a hex, seen or unseen, land or sea, and choose **Explore**: the unit sets out as an **expedition** to the land within 5 hexes of that place, for as many game days as you give it (4 to 365; 10 if you do not say).

- **First to your chosen Province.** The expedition travels to the exact hex you selected, then explores around it. If it cannot reach that hex, the order is refused; it does not substitute another destination. **After arrival, it finds its own way.** Each time it stops, it heads for the nearest ground there that none of your people has seen. **A ship keeps to the coast:** it makes for unseen coastal water before open sea, so the voyage maps the shoreline (it still sails at its usual speed). <!-- src: server/internal/combat/expedition.go nextExpeditionLeg --> You watch it go, live, but you cannot steer it — that is the point of sending it.

- **The order reserves time for the journey home.** It turns back no later than halfway through its game days, so it is home by the end of them. It turns sooner if nothing in the area is left unseen, or if what is left cannot be reached. You are told when it turns, and why. If its home is lost during the expedition, it seeks another reachable city of yours; its mission line then shows the actual return game day. Without a reachable home it stops where it is.

- **It reports when it is home**: which city it came home to, how long it was out, how far it went, how much it saw, and what it found — copper, tin, silver and cedar, and the foreign cities on the way.
- An expedition into ground you already know all of is refused, and so is one too short to reach the chosen hex and come back.

- A Runner that recalls it turns it home at once; it still files its report on arrival, covering what it saw so far. A Runner that redirects it ends the expedition; it then behaves like any other march.

- Out in the field it eats double, from home, like any unit away from its city ([[upkeep]]). A ship takes on food for every game day of the expedition before it sails ([[sea]]).
