The oracle rite reveals ore deposits you cannot see — see [[rites]]. Seeing a city does not open trade with it — that takes [[contact]].

Rivers begin unnamed. The first Wanax whose own physical unit reaches a river earns the right to name it; seeing it gives no right. The river, its fords and connected delta share the chosen name. A named river appears in its known hex panels, map label and Keryx catchment rows. Unexplored hexes reveal no name or naming right; remembered ground keeps its name visible. See [[naming-the-land]] for the naming action and the other kinds of land.

When an expedition turns home, its dispatch says **Mission complete** and gives an estimated local clock arrival. The estimate follows the current world clock; the expedition report preserves its findings.
Sight determines which ground and moving people you can currently see.
You see the world at two depths: what you are looking at **now**, and what you **remember**.
A few things are not yours to choose. They are not treaties and no one signs them; they are how the world works.

A herald cannot be attacked. No army, raider or Wanax can intercept a messenger, on the way out or on the way home. A letter always reaches its city unless the sea itself takes the runner. See [[messengers]].
A runner who reaches a harbour without a ship of his own boards whatever ship sails his way, **yours or another Wanax's**. No one refuses a herald passage. See [[messengers]] and [[sea]].

When a ship reaches a city, its own or another Wanax's, the city gives it food for the voyage home. It is free and needs no consent. The port first keeps enough for its own people's daily meal and gives only what it can spare. See [[ship-food-return]].

When a Wanax's last city falls and they [[last-city|rise again]], their survivors are suppliants, under the gods' protection until they found a city. You may still attack their Nomadic Host or its escort. If a battle against them actually begins, **your realm loses 70 kharis** (never below the floor of 1). A march that never reaches them costs nothing. Once they have founded a city, the protection ends.

Before an order against a host you can see goes out, you are warned: in the march panel, **March anyway** sends it; in [[keryx|Keryx]], add `--confirm` to `keryx unit march`. No one else is told; your own kharis shows the loss in **Kult**.

The gods keep an order among the Wanaxes even when they are rivals. The Greeks of a later age called it **themis**: what is right because the gods hold it so. Its oldest part is **xenia**, the bond between host and guest.
**Rumour is not contact.** [[gossip|Gossip]] tells you that a city exists and roughly where, deliberately blurred, but it does not open the door. Seeing a city on the map ([[sight]]) does not either.
Cities you have contacted appear in **Diplomacy → Letters → Write**. Choose **Write** to ask their Wanax what they need or can spare; market knowledge comes through [[messengers|correspondence]].
Contact reveals that city’s location, not the surrounding land or its current activity.

**A letter you receive tells you who wrote, not where they live.** It opens no contact and puts nothing on your map. You can still answer it — your reply goes home with the same runner while it waits.

Opening a letter in an exchange marks it as read. The Diplomacy badge counts unread letters; an unanswered offer can remain pending after you have read it. `keryx inbox` marks the letters it displays as read too. Reading does not send the messenger home or accept a trade.
Received letters remain in Letters after the runner leaves or an offer closes. Use `keryx inbox --history` to read past correspondence; plain `keryx inbox` lists current messages and pending offers.
You cannot write to, or trade with, a city you have never reached. A settlement becomes reachable — **permanently** — once one of these has happened:
Contact is earned by walking, and once earned it never lapses. Sending a messenger to a stranger's city is not only a letter — it is the act that opens [[trade]] with them for good.

Open the dispatch to read the whole sealed contents: the letter and any reply, the trade proposal or the order, its recorded departure time (for example, "Sent yesterday 18:34"), and its origin and destination. The record does not change when cities or orders change later.
A lost runner cannot deliver the message later. Sending again is your decision. If another ship rescues it, see [[runner-rescued-at-sea]].
An older sealed record may have no preserved departure game day; it says "Sent on an unknown game day" rather than guessing.

The dispatch names people first: "From you, at Mycenae, to Wanax Oledoledoff at Tiryns." An order names "your Bronze Guard at (9, 4)" instead. The recipient's public Wanax name, your unit's name and the places are preserved when the runner is lost; later name changes do not rewrite the sealed record. Account logins are not used.

The headline names only the recipient: "Your runner to Wanax Oledoledoff at Tiryns was lost at sea in a storm." For an order: "Your runner to your Bronze Guard at (9, 4) was lost at sea in a storm." The full origin stays in the sealed envelope below.
# A runner lost at sea

A storm can sink a runner's ship. If a ship sinks in battle and no enemy ship survives to rescue the runner, the runner is lost too. This applies to [[messengers|letters]], trade offers and [[runners|orders]].
If the crew disappears from [[upkeep|hunger or desertion]], the runner steps ashore if it can reach a nearby settlement. Out at sea, with no way to leave, it is lost.
You learn immediately that **your own runner was lost**. This is the one exception to news needing a physical bearer. The dispatch tells you nothing else about the battle or other people’s ships.
You receive no instant rescue news or location. Your outbox says **no word**, and the runner's unknown position gives you no map marker or sight. The recipient simply receives the message later.

The report says when the runner came home, such as "Home today 18:34". When the runner comes home with its answer, it brings its own account of the rescue ship and the port where it landed. A one-way order runner does not send a report home from afar. Only [[runner-lost-at-sea|loss]] is reported immediately. See [[sea]] and [[messengers]].

The account names the ship and the actual towns in a sentence: "Home today 18:34. Your runner was rescued at sea by the Sacred Dolphin and put ashore at Tiryns, then went ashore at Mycenae." With only one landing: "Home today 18:34. Your runner was rescued at sea by the Sacred Dolphin and put ashore at Tiryns." The town names are preserved when the runner steps ashore.
# A runner rescued at sea

A herald is sacred. When its ship sinks in battle, a surviving enemy ship takes the runner aboard. A captured ship also keeps its runner safe, even though its owner has changed. The new owner cannot read the sealed message or hold the runner captive.

The runner follows that **actual ship to its next port**, steps ashore and continues toward the original destination. It may need to wait for another passage. A damaged ship that survives and turns home keeps its runner aboard until that home port; that is neither a loss nor a rescue.

**Letters** has one row per Wanax: their name, the last line of the latest letter, and **Waiting on you**, **Waiting on them** or **Done**. Letters awaiting your answer come first, with the nearest deadline first. An unanswered offer remains actionable even when you cannot afford its payment.

Open a Wanax to read your exchange, oldest first. The newest letter is open; expand an older letter to read it. Opening a letter marks it read. Reading never accepts a trade or sends an answer. Offers have **Accept** and **Decline** buttons. An accepted offer remains in the exchange as **Agreed**, with its exact terms; agreement does not prove the goods have arrived.

The reply box sits below the exchange. **Send with their runner** uses the bearer waiting for your answer and shows when he leaves. **Send a runner** sends a new letter to a city you have contacted. **Write** lists the Wanax you can reach, with their contacted cities beneath. A rumour does not open a route. You can also write from a known city's Inspect panel. Unsent text stays in the box in this browser while you use the drawer; it is not saved to the server.

Keryx: `letters` lists your correspondents; `letters "Myrine"` reads your exchange with that Wanax. `--json` returns the same data. `reply --id <letter-id> --text "..."` answers with the waiting bearer. `message --to <city> --text "..."` sends a new runner; `trade-offer` attaches structured trade terms. `inbox` remains available for received letters and marks those displayed as read.

A letter to a distant city takes game days, and the reply takes as long again. You are told when your messenger arrives, and again when he is home with the answer. Plan diplomacy the way you plan a march.

A reply uses the **same bearer** who brought the letter. You can return a letter even if you have not discovered the sender's city; answering does not create a new messenger or reveal that city's location.

A newly delivered plain letter can be answered on its arrival game day and the following game day. The bearer leaves at the start of the next game day. **Letters** shows the departure time with the local departure time. Once the return-post window closes, you cannot reply through that bearer, even while his departure is still being processed. Reading does not extend his stay. A previously issued longer stay keeps its saved deadline. Trade offers keep their own answer deadline.

If nobody replies, your messenger does not wait forever in that city's court. After a while he gives up and turns around on his own, walking home just as he would with an answer in hand — the same road, taking the same time. You are still told the moment he is back, only without a reply riding along.

**A messenger cannot be intercepted** — not on the way out, not on the way home. A herald is sacred and everyone knows it. It is the one thing on the map that is immune, which is why letters are the reliable backbone of everything you do at a distance. See [[xenia]] for the gods' order behind it.
A [[runners|Runner]] carrying an order is sacred too. Armies and goods are not. At sea, holiness protects a bearer from people, not a storm: see [[runner-lost-at-sea]] and [[runner-rescued-at-sea]].
The first letter you send to a city also opens [[contact]] with it for good.
A messenger cannot swim any more than a Runner can. When a letter's road crosses open water it waits in your own port for a ship instead — see [[sea]] for how the crossing actually works.

If an order Runner is waiting for a ship, open its dispatch to see the sealed order's unit, destination and mission. Your Notifications history keeps those details readable after the Runner moves. Only your own order is shown; another Wanax's Runner does not reveal its envelope.
A **messenger** walks your letter to another Wanax and brings the answer home. **Diplomacy (✉)** has two tabs: **Letters** and **Runners**.

Rumours appear in the same list as your notifications, newest first, each marked **Rumour** with a 🗣 so you can tell what you have only heard from what happened to you. The rulers you know are listed under **Known** in Diplomacy.
Use gossip to decide where to send a messenger or a scout; use [[sight]] and [[contact]] to act on it.

An omen is a true observation when it is given, rather than a promise about the future. It may point to a storm, metal-bearing ground, or the current balance between food production and the townsfolk's meals. When there is no true sign to convey, the gods remain silent. Later movement or work can change what was observed.

Higher Kharis brings signs more often, from farther away, and with more detail. Below 5 the minimum gap is 12 game days; at 5, 30, 60 and 90 it falls to 8, 5, 3 and 2 game days. These are minimum gaps, not promises that a sign will appear. A modest temple cannot reach the highest standing: a level 3 temple can support Kharis 100. Near Kharis 90 or above, a rare urgent coastal storm omen can name a concrete hex; it never gives an exact force, future arrival time or route. Low standing never reveals that precise hex. Names of unknown cities are not revealed.
Omens have their own star marker in Notifications. Your own goods movements are not told back to you as trade rumours.
**Gossip (🗣)** is what travellers, merchants and soldiers say about the world beyond your sight — who rules where, what happened, which cities exist.
Rumour is useful but blurred:
Every ship needs a **Harbour** and a **Shipyard** ([[buildings]]). There are three kinds ([[units|Forces]]):

- **Galley** — 30 timber, no silver to build or maintain. Transport and sight at sea. Can carry goods.
- **War Galley** — the warship. Needs cedar and a Foundry. Never carries cargo.
- **Emporos** — a trade hull built with 90 cedar, no timber or silver. It draws no silver pay. It is no warship (1 die in battle, like a Galley), but carries more than a Galley.

A [[transfers|transfer]] or [[routes|standing order]] that goes by sea needs a free Galley or Emporos waiting in the sending port — the War Galley is never chosen. No free hull there, and the shipment goes by land instead if a road exists, or is refused.

correction.replacement: A [[transfers|transfer]] or [[routes|standing order]] that goes by sea needs a free Galley or Emporos waiting in the sending port — the War Galley is never chosen. With automatic routing, no free hull means land instead if a route exists, or refusal. An explicitly chosen sea route never switches to land.

records.text: **Lay up** an idle, empty ship in your own active Harbour from War → Forces when you do not need it. The crew joins the port's population, so the ship costs no food or silver and cannot sail, carry goods or take a passenger. **Fit out** drafts its crew again and takes three game days before the ship is ready. The crew draws home-rate food and, for War Galleys, half field pay while fitting out. A laid-up hull follows its port if the city is annexed. See [[units|Forces]] and [[upkeep]].

records.section: Carry troops to your own city
records.text: In **War → Forces**, use **Load** for each cohort you want aboard, then **March** and choose your own coastal city or harbour on the map or in **Destination city**. A Galley or War Galley takes one land unit; an Emporos takes up to three.

records.section: Carry troops to your own city
records.text: The ship sails to the city and docks there. **Everyone aboard joins that city's garrison automatically**, and **the ship stays in its harbour**. You do not need a second Unload order. An empty ship can sail to the same city and stay there. The ship and troops keep their existing supporting city; docking does not transfer who pays their upkeep. **The ship takes provisions for its next voyage from the harbour where it is actually docked**, for ordinary missions as well as freight. A distant supporting city's food cannot supply this departure.

records.section: Carry troops to your own city
records.text: Keryx: `unit march --unit <ship-id> --to "Petras"`. A laden ship can also use `--intent land` for your own city. For a foreign coastal city, an ordinary march by a laden ship uses the existing amphibious assault; Land does not attack a foreign city. **Land on open, unclaimed ground** still puts everyone ashore and sends the ship home, with optional colony founding. Ships take these orders before departure from port.

- **A ship is given its whole mission in port, then sails alone.** From **War → Forces**, **Load** a land unit onto a ship standing with it (a Galley or War Galley takes one, an [[emporos|Emporos]] up to three), then send it on a **mission**: **Land** puts everyone aboard ashore on open ground and sails home again on its own — select "…and found a colony" to settle right there, no further order needed; the unit loaded first founds it and the others stand beside it. The port pays the colonists' silver the moment the ship sails, as it would for a column on foot ([[colonies]]); if the colony cannot be founded, or you unload them at home, the silver comes back with them. **Patrol** and **Explore** return home by themselves. For **Explore**, choose an area and duration in game days: the port loads provisions for the whole expedition, and the ship turns home by half the duration ([[sight]]). **Passage** is a fourth mission, empty of cargo, given to carry a [[messengers|letter]] or [[runners|order]] — see "Arrange passage" below.

- **Once it sails, a ship takes no more orders.** March, Recall, Redirect, Stance, Load, Unload — none of them reach a ship that isn't standing in its own port. This is the messenger pillar taken to its edge: nothing reaches a ship at sea, not even you. Give the whole mission before it leaves; its mission determines whether it comes home or stays docked in your destination city.
- **Sight.** A ship reads the open sea out to four hexes but sees only one hex inland.

- **Crew pay.** Only War Galley rowers draw silver: 1 silver per hundred rowers per game day in the field, half at home — **0.5 / 0.25** for a full crew. Galley and Emporos crews draw no silver pay. Repairs and fitting out count as home; marching, posted and freight missions count as field service, including waits between freight legs. A laid-up ship draws no pay. Carried soldiers draw their own field pay ([[upkeep]]).

- **Supplies.** Rowers eat the same per-person ration as spearmen, doubled while marching, posted or freighting ([[upkeep]]). The actual surviving crew determines the ration, and any carried soldiers need their own field rations too. A crew eats grain, fish, oil and wine, with the same proportional sharing as the city. The port loads food for the voyage from these four goods; livestock is not ship provision. War → Forces shows food for N game days and the goods aboard, including ships carrying goods on a freight route and waiting between its legs. Keryx `unit list` shows the same supply. Unused provisions come home as the goods that were loaded, so fish does not turn into grain. A ship turns home before its food runs too low for the voyage back, unless it can reach a city for provisions. You hear why when it reaches home; see [[ship-food-return]]. Ports feed visiting ships as guests; see [[xenia]]. At sea it eats only what was loaded aboard, never from a city's granary. The food gauge counts whole game days; "less than a game day" means the last ration is being eaten, "out of food" means nothing is left.

The open sea is never quite safe, but **you can see its storms** — see [[storms]]. A storm is three sea hexes of dark cloud that drift slowly across the Thalassa; a ship that crosses any of them takes the damage, even between the game day's start and end, whatever the ship is doing — a fleet, a ship carrying an army, an expedition, a galley carrying a trade, a transfer or a gift. A storm can also drift onto a slow ship. Whose ship it is and why it sails never change that. Rivers and land have no storms. <!-- src: server/internal/combat/sea_storm_weather.go SeaHexesPerStorm -->

- **Each storm costs the ship two points of hull** (of five), once, however many game days it spends inside that storm. Three storms sink a ship that began with full hull. You are told where it struck and how much hull is left.
- **At hull 0 the ship founders.** It goes down with everything aboard: its crew, any troops it carries, and any cargo. You are told where, and what was lost with her.
- A battered ship keeps sailing. Bring it home and **Repair** it at a Shipyard before its next long voyage.

Ships are damaged in [[battle]] and by storms. A damaged ship can be **Repaired** at a Shipyard (**War → Forces → Repair**); you are notified when the work is done. Ships can also be lost at sea outright — and the gods, when angry, sometimes take one from the harbour ([[kharis]]).

A ship caught carrying cargo (see [[transfers]]) can also be **captured outright** — it changes hands on the spot and sails to the raider's nearest port under its new flag. If your own trade route's home port is gone by the time a ship comes back — burned, occupied, abandoned — it docks at your next-nearest settlement instead; with none left anywhere, it sits **stranded** wherever it made landfall until you give it a fresh order.

records.section: Hitching a ride — how a letter or an order crosses the sea
records.text: A [[messengers|letter]] or a [[runners|Runner]] carrying your order cannot swim, and it never guesses at a crossing — it needs a real ship, full stop. When its road crosses open water:

records.section: Hitching a ride — how a letter or an order crosses the sea
records.text: - It runs to **your own nearest coastal or harboured city** and waits there — you are told which one, and why. If you have no coastal or harboured city anywhere, the message is refused outright at the moment you send it, rather than dispatched to wait forever.

records.section: Hitching a ride — how a letter or an order crosses the sea
records.text: - The moment **any** ship or trade route — yours or another Wanax's — sails from that port toward the right side of the sea, it **boards** — free, no cargo space taken — and steps off wherever that ship lands, then finishes the trip on foot. Runners are sacred: every captain takes them aboard, even between Wanaxes at war. It only boards a ship that lands it **nearer its goal** than the port it waits in — a ship bound the wrong way, it lets sail. The runner never changes where the ship goes, and the ship's owner sees only that a runner of yours is aboard, never what it carries.

records.section: Hitching a ride — how a letter or an order crosses the sea
records.text: - A storm can [[runner-lost-at-sea|lose the runner]]. In battle a surviving enemy ship [[runner-rescued-at-sea|rescues it]]; a captured ship keeps it aboard. It leaves that actual ship in its next port and continues. A damaged ship that survives takes its runner home to the next port, without sealing or loss.

records.section: Hitching a ride — how a letter or an order crosses the sea
records.text: - If no ship sails that way for a while, it simply keeps waiting — nothing crosses on its own. See "A runner stuck waiting" below for what you can do about it.

records.section: Hitching a ride — how a letter or an order crosses the sea
records.text: None of this changes anything for a message or order whose road stays on dry land — a Runner on land never needs a ship, only [[marching|the roads]] it can already walk (a river still needs a ford or a boat of its own, unrelated to sea passage).

records.section: What the map shows while it crosses
records.text: Your own [[messengers|letter]] or [[runners|Runner]] is drawn exactly where it really is, not sailing on its own across open water:

records.section: What the map shows while it crosses
records.text:
- **Waiting** — it stands still in the port it ran to, a gold pennant marking it as yours. A small red mark on top means a **PassageStalled** dispatch has already fired for this wait.
- **Aboard** — it rides the deck of whichever ship or trade route picked it up, moving exactly when and where that ship does. Hover it to see the carrier's name.
- **Ashore** — once the ship lands it, it steps off and finishes the last stretch on foot, same as any Runner on land.
- **No word** — after a rescue its location is unknown to you: no marker, carrier name or sight. It tells you about the detour only when it physically comes home. Sealed markers remain a recovery measure for older unresolved journeys.

records.section: A runner stuck waiting — your decision, not the game's
records.text: Wait long enough with no ship sailing the right way, and you get a **PassageStalled** dispatch: the runner, the port it's standing in, where it's trying to reach, and the ships (if any) of yours already there. Nothing forces your hand — it keeps waiting exactly where it is until you act, and the dispatch only ever fires once per spell of waiting (a later known waiting spell can trigger it again; an unknown rescued runner sends no news from a foreign port). Three choices:

records.section: A runner stuck waiting — your decision, not the game's
records.text:
- **Arrange passage** — the same button as above, right there in the dispatch.
- **Call it back** — give up on this errand and bring the runner home undelivered. See the instructions below.
- **Let it wait** — close the dispatch and do nothing. It keeps waiting, exactly as it was.

records.section: Call it back — bring the runner home undelivered
records.text: In **Diplomacy → Correspondence**, use **Call it back** on the waiting runner's row, or use the same choice in its **PassageStalled** dispatch. In Keryx, find the runner with `outbox`, then use `call-back --id <messenger-id>`.

records.section: Call it back — bring the runner home undelivered
records.text: This works only for an outbound runner waiting for a ship in **your own port**. A runner already aboard a ship, or waiting in a foreign port on its return journey, cannot be called back this way — arrange passage instead.

records.section: Call it back — bring the runner home undelivered
records.text: The runner turns around and walks home over land, delivering nothing. The confirmation tells you when it will return; it is still travelling until then. A letter comes home undelivered, and an order comes home withdrawn.

records.section: Arrange passage — send a ship for your own runner
records.text: Waiting for a ship to happen to sail the right way is not your only choice. From your **outbox** (Diplomacy, or `keryx outbox`), a runner waiting for passage shows an **Arrange passage** button (or `keryx passage`) whenever one of your own ships qualifies — the choice of ship is always yours to make, but only real, eligible ships are ever offered: a Galley or Emporos (never a War Galley), standing free in port with no mission of its own.

records.section: Arrange passage — send a ship for your own runner
records.text: - **Sending one out:** the ship must stand in the SAME port the runner is waiting in. It sails straight for the runner's destination, boards it the moment it leaves, and puts it ashore there — no different from boarding any ship that happened to be going that way, except this one you chose yourself.

records.section: Arrange passage — send a ship for your own runner
records.text: - **Bringing one home:** a runner that has finished its errand and is waiting in a **foreign** port may be fetched instead — any of your own ports will do. The ship sails there, waits (**War → Forces** shows it "waiting at (…) for the runner's return", or `keryx unit` says the same), and carries the runner all the way home the moment it is ready to travel.

records.section: Arrange passage — send a ship for your own runner
records.text: - Either way, **the ship still finishes its own mission on its own** afterwards — it always sails home again, exactly like Land, Patrol or Explore. The runner never commands the ship; you send the ship for the runner, never the other way round. While it sails out, the drawer and `keryx unit` show it "carrying a runner to (…)".

records.section: Arrange passage — send a ship for your own runner
records.text: - The ship's own risks are unchanged: it can still be damaged, captured or sunk, and a starved crew still turns it for home ([[upkeep]]) — none of that touches the runner, who stands safely ashore the whole time.

records.section: Fetch home — send a ship to fetch a unit
records.text: A land [[units|unit]] stranded on another shore — landed there, or marched off on its own — cannot swim home. From that unit's own card (**Fetch by ship**, whenever one of your own ships qualifies), or `keryx unit pickup`, you send a ship to bring it back.

records.section: Fetch home — send a ship to fetch a unit
records.text: - **The shore is chosen for you.** If the unit already stands on ground a ship can reach by sea, that is the shore. Otherwise the nearest open, unclaimed coastline near it is picked automatically — never a foreign city.

records.section: Fetch home — send a ship to fetch a unit
records.text: - **A runner rides along if one is needed.** When the unit does not already stand on the chosen shore, a Runner boards the very same ship, steps ashore with it, and marches inland to order the unit to the shore — exactly like [[messengers|arrange passage]]'s own crossing, just carrying a march order instead of a letter. Only a Galley or Emporos can carry that runner; a War Galley may only fetch a unit that is already standing on the shore.

records.section: Fetch home — send a ship to fetch a unit
records.text: - **The ship waits, but not forever.** You choose how many game days it holds off the shore. If the unit reaches the shore in time, it boards at once and the ship sails home with it. If the wait runs out first, the ship sails home empty — you are told either way.

records.section: Fetch home — send a ship to fetch a unit
records.text: - **Home is the end of the errand.** The moment the ship docks, the fetched unit steps off straight into that city's garrison — no separate Unload needed.

records.section: Fetch home — send a ship to fetch a unit
records.text: None of this reaches a ship already at sea (ships take no orders once they sail — see "At sea" above): a pickup is a whole mission, given from port, same as Land, Patrol or Explore.

With a full crew, a Galley covers **3 coastal hexes** or **5 deep-sea hexes per
game day**. Rivers allow **2 hexes per game day**; a ford takes **1 game day** for a ship.
Deep water is faster, and [[storms|storms]] can still damage or sink a ship.
See [[marching]] for ship, crew and cargo modifiers and journey rounding.

For goods, a **Galley carries 20** and an **Emporos carries 120 goods of any kind**. One good takes one cargo place; several goods can share a single [[transfers|shipment]]. A ship carrying a land unit is unavailable for goods freight.
Ships carry people, messages and goods across navigable water.
The sea is **the Thalassa**. It carries your ships, your traders and your ambitions — and it is how you reach the half of [[bronze]] your own land does not have.

A river includes its fords and connected delta. A mountain massif joins neighbouring limestone and red mountains; a desert joins neighbouring desert hexes; a cedar forest joins neighbouring cedar woodland. Massifs, deserts and cedar forests must cover at least five hexes to be named. Olive groves are cultivated land and cannot be named this way.

Click any known hex of the place on the map. If the right is yours, its panel offers a name box. The right lasts until used, with no time limit. **You may name it once.** A nameless place keeps its terrain title and has no name label on the map.

Names are trimmed, 2–30 characters, and may contain letters, digits, spaces, apostrophes and hyphens. A name must be unique in the world, ignoring letter case. Naming is immediate: it sends no order or Runner.

After naming, the name appears in the hexpanel and on the map at readable zoom. The TERRAIN row still describes the ground. Only hexes you can see or remember reveal the place and its name; naming never reveals unknown land. See [[sight]].
`keryx places` lists known places, their kind and anchor id (`q,r`), their known hexes, and whether you may name them.

`keryx places name river 6,79 "Alpheios"` names a river. Use `massif`, `desert` or `forest` for the other kinds, with the id shown in your list. Add `--json` for the complete API reply. If an anchor starts with a minus sign, put `--` before the positional arguments: `keryx places name -- river -6,79 "Alpheios"`.

Administrators can change or remove unsuitable names with `keryx places rename <kind> <q,r> "<name>"` or `keryx places unname <kind> <q,r>` and their admin key. Removing a name leaves the naming right spent.
Storms follow their own rule: the first ship struck by a storm earns its naming right. See [[storms]].
# Naming the land

The first Wanax whose **own physical unit reaches** a river, mountain massif, desert or cedar forest gains the right to name it. Seeing the place nearby gives no right. You receive a notice naming the unit that reached it first.

For a river, desert or cedar forest, your unit must enter one of its hexes. For a mountain massif, your unit must enter **land directly bordering the mountains**. Mountains remain impassable. If that land borders two separate massifs, you gain the right to name both. Simply seeing mountains from farther away gives no naming right.

Each game day a storm takes **two steps**. In each step, one of its three hexes moves to a neighbouring sea hex, and the storm stays in one piece. So a storm crawls: slowly, and a little more each game day in the direction it has been drifting, now and then turning. It never crosses land.

A ship that **sails into a storm** takes two points of hull damage (of five) — once per storm, however many game days it spends inside it; three storms sink a ship from full hull. At hull 0 she founders with everything aboard ([[sea]]). A ship beside a storm is safe. Ships follow the route they were given and cannot steer round a storm once they sail ([[sea]]), so look before you send them.

Every sea hex a ship crosses is checked, even when it crosses several in one game day. Two different storms crossed that game day each strike; staying inside the same storm gives no extra blow. A storm can also drift onto a slow ship. [[rites|Favourable Passage]] still protects the ship on its outward leg.
A storm standing on a city's fishing hex stops the fishing there until it moves on ([[fishing]]).
You see a storm **only inside your own sight** ([[sight]]) — from your cities, your ships and your soldiers. There it is drawn as dark cloud, and hovering tells you which way it is drifting.

Once you have seen a storm, the map remembers it **where you last saw it**, as a faded cloud, and hovering says on which game day. That is not where it is now. If you see any part of that place and the storm is not there, it has moved on and the memory is dropped.

The first Wanax whose ship a storm strikes **may name it**, once — even if that blow sinks the ship. You are told in the storm notice. Click the storm on the map and give it a name (2 to 30 letters, digits, spaces, apostrophes and hyphens; no two storms share a name). The storm keeps the name wherever it drifts, and everyone who sees or remembers it will see the name. A name that is out of order can be changed or removed by the game's keepers; the one who gave it does not get a second try.
In Keryx: `storms` lists the storms in sight and the ones you remember, with their ids; `storms name <id> "<name>"` names one you were first to meet.

**Fishers stay at their grounds.** A storm makes them catch nothing while it covers their hex; it never sends them home or removes their placement. They resume fishing when it moves on. See [[fishing]].

A **storm** is three connected hexes of dark cloud on the Thalassa. There is about one for every 100 hexes of sea, and they never stop wandering. <!-- src: server/internal/combat/sea_storm_weather.go SeaHexesPerStorm -->

**War → Recruit.** Choose the city at the top if you hold several. Each row shows the total cost of one order and how many men or crew it drafts from the city. An unavailable row keeps that price visible and names what is missing, including the required amount and what the city has.

| Force | Needs | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **[[spearmen|Spearman]]** | Barracks | The levy. 12 grain for one 100-man cohort; no silver. |
| **[[elite-infantry|Bronze Guard]]** | Barracks + Foundry | Costs [[bronze]]. Far harder per man. |
| **[[war-chariot|Chariot]]** | Stable | Costs bronze. The hardest hitter on the field. |
| **[[galley|Galley]]** | Shipyard | 30 timber (or cedar); no silver. Transport and sight at sea ([[sea]]). |
| **[[war-galley|War Galley]]** | Shipyard + Foundry | Costs cedar. The warship. |
| **[[emporos|Emporos]]** | Shipyard | 90 cedar; no timber or silver. Trade hull; carries the most goods and up to three land forces, no warship. |

Timber costs can be paid with cedar, one for one. Timber is used first; cedar fills the shortfall. Cedar specifically required by an order must still be available before any spare cedar can cover timber.

Land forces train as a whole hundred-man cohort (**Train 100**). Ships are built one at a time and can be named. Their cost and population draft cover the ship's crew, rather than a hundred-man cohort. Rowers eat like spearmen: the actual surviving crew draws a port ration at home and double on a mission ([[upkeep]]). Rejected recruitment consumes no people or goods. The completion dispatch names the ready unit type and its city — for example, “Emporos ready in Tylissos”. **Show the ship** or **Review the unit** opens its highlighted Forces card. If the unit no longer exists, the dispatch does not offer an empty unit view. A cohort still gathering men or training cannot march. Once ready, it can still march after losing men; it does not have to refill to 100 first.

Every cohort is numbered by its home city: **2nd Spearmen of Knossos**. A lost regiment's number is never given out again. Before you found your first city, your [[horde]]'s two escort cohorts carry your own name instead — **1st** and **2nd Spearmen of** *you* — and become the new city's 1st and 2nd when you settle.

A cohort is drafted out of your city's population and stays out of it until disbanded. Soldiers still eat. **Spearmen, Galleys and Emporoi draw 0 silver per game day**. Bronze Guard, chariots and War Galleys draw pay in [[silver]]. Home service costs half field pay: a full elite cohort draws 0.75 / 1.5 silver per game day at home / in the field, and a full chariot cohort 2 / 4. A full War Galley draws 0.25 / 0.5 ([[upkeep]]). An army bigger than your city can feed and pay is not a strong army; it is a famine with spears.

In each combat round, **100 active spearmen roll 50 dice**. Half the active men roll, rounded up: one man rolls one die, three roll two. Bronze Guard rolls three dice per active man and chariots five per chariot. A **War Galley rolls 5 dice**, against a **Galley's 1** before hull damage and other battle adjustments.

**Disband** selects a whole unit by name in City → Garrison. Its remaining people return to that city: a full Spearmen cohort returns 100 people; a damaged cohort returns only its survivors. There is no soldier-quantity input. Ships return their actual crew; a laid-up hull returns no crew a second time. Keryx: `disband --unit "<unit name>"` or `disband --unit <unit-id> --province <city>`; repeat `--unit` to select several whole forces in that city. The receipt names each unit before its returned people and city: “2nd Spearmen of Phaistos disbanded — 41 people return to Phaistos.” Selecting several forces gives one sentence per unit. Silver is unchanged.

An empty ship in your own active Harbour can be **Laid up** from its Forces card. Its crew returns to the port's population and can work there; the hull draws no food or silver and remains in port. The card says **Laid up** and offers **Fit out**. Fitting out takes the ship's full crew from that city's current population and prepares it for **three game days**. It cannot sail or be cancelled during that time, and its crew draws home-rate food and, for a War Galley, half field pay from the start. If the city is annexed, its laid-up and fitting-out ships go with the city. Disbanding a laid-up ship removes the hull without returning the same crew twice; choose the particular hull to disband by its name. Keryx: `unit lay-up --unit ID` and `unit fit-out --unit ID`.

Every unit you own, with its state and current grain and silver upkeep per game day in plain words. **March** is shown while it can move; a damaged land cohort garrisoned in its **original home city** can also **Reinforce** — another city you own does not qualify. A land unit on the march shows **Recall**. The card also shows stance and **Set**, battle retreat, **Redirect**, **Fetch by ship**, **Load** / **Unload** or **Repair**, whenever that unit can use them. Choose **Destination city** in a march or redirect form to target a known city quickly; map clicks remain available. Keryx accepts `--to "City name"` on march, post and redirect. See [[marching]], [[stances]] and [[sea]].

**Marches** lists your forces on the march (**Outgoing**) and every foreign unit you can see marching on one of your settlements (**Incoming**), soonest arrival first. You only see an incoming column once one of your eyes has it in sight — the *foreign march sighted* notification fires at the same moment ([[defence]]).
