records.text: Recruitment confirms that your order was received. While a unit is still training, use **Cancel training** in War → Forces to return its people and reserved resources. A ship under construction has **Cancel build**. In Keryx use `unit cancel-training --unit ID`. Finished forces use Disband instead.

For goods, a **Galley carries 20** and an **Emporos carries 120 goods of any kind**. One good takes one cargo place; several goods can share a single [[transfers|shipment]]. A ship carrying a land unit is unavailable for goods freight.

**Forces** groups your roster as **Land Forces**, **Ships** and, only while you
have a Nomadic Host, **People**. Being in harbour, marching, aboard another
ship or laid up is shown on each card. A ship bound to a standing route stays
under Ships and names its route, including between legs.

**Marches** lists your ordered marches, sailings, landings, expeditions and
returns, together with known incoming threats. Automated trade is under
**Economy → Routes & cargo**, where each standing route shows its travelling
ship or caravan. Other shipments, including agreements, transfers and gifts,
have their own cargo list there. See [[routes]] and [[transfers]].

`keryx forces` shows the same roster. Older `units`, `army` and `unit list`
commands remain accepted.
Forces are the soldiers, ships and people you command.
The **War (⚔)** drawer has three tabs: **Forces**, **Recruit** and **Marches**.

The **Galley** is the ordinary ship: built of timber, rowed by twenty, the hull that carries your people and your goods across the [[sea|Thalassa]].

| | |
|---|---|
| **Built at** | Shipyard ([[shipyard]]) |
| **Cost for one ship** | 30 timber (or cedar) · no silver |
| **Crew** | 20 rowers, drafted from the city |
| **Build time** | 3 game days |
| **Food** | 0.1 per game day in port, 0.2 at sea |
| **Pay** | none |
| **Cargo** | 20 goods of any kind ([[transfers]]) |
| **Troops** | one land unit at a time, any size |
| **Speed** | ordinary |
| **Hull** | 5; repaired with timber (or cedar) |
| **In battle** | 1 die per round, weaker as the hull is damaged |

A galley is what most realms sail first. It can carry a cohort to a new shore and [[colonies|found a colony]] there, take a [[messengers|messenger]] across the water, explore, patrol or run a freight route. It does not fight well; for that, build a [[war-galley]]. For bulk trade, the [[emporos]] carries six times as much.

See [[units|Forces]] for recruiting and [[sea]] for missions, storms and supplies.

A War Galley is not a thicker or better-armoured ship. It is dangerous because of who is aboard: rowers, archers, slingers and boarding fighters — a trained marine force, not ordinary oarsmen or soldiers carried as passengers. In a sea fight it shoots at the enemy from a distance, then closes to board or force a surrender. That is why it rolls 5 dice where a Galley or an Emporos rolls 1.
It is also why only the War Galley costs silver and draws pay. A Galley or an Emporos is rowed by ordinary men from the city; a War Galley keeps standing marines.

So it is a costly specialist. It strikes hard and is the fastest ship at sea, but it has the same 5 hull points as any other hull. Three Galleys roll fewer dice together, yet carry three times the hull — a real danger to it, more so once it is damaged.
Build it when ships must fight or hunt other ships. It carries no cargo, so trade stays with the [[galley]] and the [[emporos]]. See [[units|Forces]] and [[battle]].
The **War Galley** is the warship: cedar-built, fifty at the oars, fast and dangerous.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Built at** | Shipyard + Foundry |
| **Cost for one ship** | 100 cedar · 30 silver |
| **Crew** | 50 rowers, drafted from the city |
| **Build time** | 5 game days |
| **Food** | 0.25 per game day in port, 0.5 at sea |
| **Pay** | 0.25 silver per game day at home, 0.5 at sea ([[silver]]) |
| **Cargo** | no goods |
| **Troops** | one land unit at a time |
| **Speed** | fastest ship — 0.6 of a galley's travel time |
| **Hull** | 5; repaired with cedar |
| **In battle** | 5 dice per round against a [[galley]]'s 1, weaker as the hull is damaged |

The **Emporos** is the merchant hull: broad, slow, cedar-built, made to carry.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Built at** | Shipyard |
| **Cost for one ship** | 90 cedar · no timber, no silver |
| **Crew** | 10 rowers, drafted from the city |
| **Build time** | 4 game days |
| **Food** | 0.05 per game day in port, 0.1 at sea |
| **Pay** | none |
| **Cargo** | 120 goods of any kind ([[transfers]]) |
| **Troops** | up to three land forces at once — passengers, not fighters: they roll no dice at sea and drown if she founders |
| **Speed** | slowest ship — 1.4 times a galley's travel time |
| **Hull** | 5; repaired with cedar |
| **In battle** | 1 die per round, like a [[galley]] — it is no warship |

When a shipment is too heavy for a [[galley]], the Emporos takes it; freight picks an Emporos before a galley when both stand in port. It needs cedar, which not every coast has ([[goods]]). See [[units|Forces]], [[sea]] and [[trade]].

**Spearmen** are the levy: a hundred of your own people with spears and shields. Cheap, quick to raise, and the backbone of every army.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Trained at** | Barracks |
| **Cost for one cohort** | 12 grain · no silver |
| **Size** | 100 men, drafted from the city |
| **Training** | 1 game day |
| **Food** | 0.5 per game day at home, 1 in the field |
| **Pay** | none |
| **In battle** | 50 dice per round for 100 active men — half the men, rounded up |

Spearmen hold walls, escort colonists and form the mass of a field army. Against [[elite-infantry|Bronze Guard]] and [[war-chariot|chariots]] they lose man for man, but they cost no [[bronze]] and no silver. See [[units|Forces]], [[marching]] and [[battle]].

**Bronze Guard** are bronze-armed warriors: few, costly, and three times as deadly as spearmen man for man.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Trained at** | Barracks + Foundry |
| **Cost for one cohort** | 24 grain · 16 [[bronze]] · 40 silver |
| **Size** | 100 men, drafted from the city |
| **Training** | 4 game days |
| **Food** | 0.6 per game day at home, 1.2 in the field |
| **Pay** | 0.75 silver per game day at home, 1.5 in the field ([[silver]]) |
| **In battle** | 3 dice per active man per round |

Bronze is the gate: no foundry, copper and tin, no elite. See [[units|Forces]], [[bronze]] and [[battle]].

The **Chariot** is the hardest hitter on open ground: horses, a driver and a warrior, built with cedar and bronze.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Built at** | Stable |
| **Cost for one cohort** | 40 grain · 8 timber (or cedar) · 8 cedar · 20 [[bronze]] · 50 silver |
| **Size** | 100 chariots |
| **Training** | 3 game days |
| **Food** | 0.8 per game day at home, 1.6 in the field |
| **Pay** | 2 silver per game day at home, 4 in the field ([[silver]]) |
| **In battle** | 5 dice per chariot per round |

Chariots need cedar and bronze both, and their pay is the highest in the army. See [[units|Forces]], [[upkeep]] and [[battle]].

**Right-click the destination hex.** The order menu shows what the destination is, which of your forces can go and **March →**. Only one unit is selected initially. Select the checkbox beside each named unit you want to order; forces sharing a type or location are separate choices. **More** holds stance ([[stances]]), expedition duration and column name.
You can also left-click a hex and use **March here →** — or **Send galleys →** at sea, or **Colonize →** on empty land ([[colonies]]). Hovering those buttons previews the result on the map.

Choose the named forces to send and the menu estimates each selected unit’s arrival **before you send the order**. **War → Forces → March** selects that unit; click a destination on the map to open the same menu. Ships with different crews or cargo may arrive at different times. The estimate uses the current route and speed; conditions can change before arrival.

If a messenger must first deliver the order, or the destination is unexplored, the forecast says why arrival is not yet known. Redirects also wait for a messenger; their current course continues until delivery. The **Sold** line shows the selected forces’ silver drain at home and in the field, and how long their paying city’s treasury lasts after departure; with several paying cities, it shows the shortest treasury duration; spearmen show **0 → 0**. No forecast sends an order.

In Keryx, use `march --unit <id> --target q,r --preview` (or `unit march` with the same flags). Add `--json` for the server forecast. Omit `--preview` when you are ready to send. `--unit` also accepts an exact unit name, for example `--unit "3rd Spearmen of Tylissos"`; names are case-insensitive and an ambiguous name is refused.

**Choose a city quickly:** the order menu's **Destination city** list offers your own cities first, followed by cities you have actually seen, remembered or contacted. Selecting one fills the destination; you can still choose a hex on the map. A city known only through rumours is not a destination yet. The confirmation names the city.

In Keryx, `march --unit <id> --to "Pylos"` chooses that city's exact hex. The same shortcut works for `unit march`, `unit post` and `unit redirect`, including march previews. Use `--to`, `--target q,r` or `--q/--r`, one form at a time. If two known cities share a name, Keryx lists the candidates and asks for coordinates. An unknown city name is refused. Selecting a city does not change which missions are valid there: a patrol still needs coastal water, so patrol has no city shortcut.
A notification tells you when a unit arrives.

records.section: A marching unit is still reachable
records.text: Right-click a new destination and a unit already marching shows up in the menu too, marked **on the march → redirect by messenger**. Pick it like any other unit — the order is a **Redirect**, not a fresh march: the unit keeps going on its old course until the Runner reaches it, then turns onto the new one. You can also redirect from the unit’s **War → Forces** row, including by typed coordinates.

records.section: Orders to forces already in the field travel by Runner
records.text: A unit standing in its city hears you at once. A unit out in the field does not — **Recall** and **Redirect** are carried by a [[runners|Runner]], and the game estimates his next meeting with the unit. The horn sounds when the soldiers *receive* the order, not when you give it.

records.section: Orders to forces already in the field travel by Runner
records.text: Recall turns an expedition home to its city, where it rejoins the garrison and files its report ([[sight]]). An ordinary march returns to its departure hex. Redirect sends the unit to the destination you choose.

records.section: Orders to forces already in the field travel by Runner
records.text: **War → Forces → Recall all**, or `keryx recall --all`, sends a separate recall order to each of your marching forces.

records.section: Orders to forces already in the field travel by Runner
records.text: Recall and redirect need a passable route from the unit’s current position. If its position or the new route cannot be resolved, the order is refused with a reason. If the Runner cannot catch up during the march, it goes to the destination. For a newly sent land order, if the unit has moved again, the Runner keeps the same order and takes a new physical route to catch it. The order takes effect only when they meet. While the Runner follows a moving unit, **War → Forces** and `keryx unit list` show the next meeting estimate, which can change; it is not a guaranteed delivery time. If the Runner must wait before continuing, they show that instead of a delivery time. A destroyed unit or a unit you no longer own cannot receive the order. A Runner-delivered refusal appears in Dispatches; the unit keeps its existing course. Check the unit and choose a reachable destination.

- **A plain march only reaches ground your people have already seen.** Right-click an unseen hex and the order menu offers **Explore** instead — the unit explores the surrounding area and returns home with a report ([[sight]]).
- Crossing the sea needs ships ([[sea]]).
- A march that cannot go on — its path blocked, or impossible — stalls, and you are told why.

A journey starts when the unit receives its order. It stays on its starting hex until it reaches the next one, then advances hex by hex along its saved route. Terrain sets the relative time between steps; the total journey keeps its rounded duration. The map and **Keryx → unit list** show the hex it has reached and its planned arrival time. Sight opens as your people advance, and storms or enemies can stop them on the way.

A marching army eats more than one in garrison and cannot forage ([[upkeep]]). It is seen by anyone whose [[sight]] it passes through, and an enemy on watch may stop it — and a [[battle]] begins by itself. **There is no declaration of war.**

Choose **Explore** in the map menu; the default expedition duration is ready to use. Open **More** to change the duration in **game days**. The chosen hex is the centre of an area, even in fog. The order summary shows its extent and duration before sending; **War → Forces → March** offers the same controls.

It travels first to the exact hex you chose, even if that hex is already seen, then chooses nearby unexplored ground on its own. It turns home by half the duration. It can turn earlier if the area is already explored or nothing further is reachable. **War → Forces** and `keryx unit list` show the area, duration, latest turn and home game day, and why it has turned. A Runner-delivered order begins when received, so those game days become known when it starts. On return, Dispatches carries the report ([[sight]]).

The chosen hex is the first destination. If it cannot be reached from this unit's position, the order is refused without substituting another destination. Choose a reachable hex or use a unit departing from elsewhere. After reaching the chosen hex, a ship prefers unseen coastal water over open sea.

In Keryx: `unit march --unit <id> --target q,r --intent explore --ticks N`. Omit `--ticks` for the server's default duration; the current allowed range comes from the game. Add `--preview` to check the order without dispatching. Exploration routes cross unknown ground, so their arrival forecast stays unavailable.

For foot soldiers, each plain, river valley or delta takes **1 game day**; olive groves
and maquis **1.5 game days**; hills and cedar forest **2 game days**; semi-desert **3 game days**.
A ford takes **2.5 game days** on foot. Mountains cannot be crossed.
Chariots are fast on the flat and slow everywhere else: **0.67 game days** on a
plain, river valley or delta, **2 game days** in olive groves and maquis, and
**3 game days** in hills, cedar forest and semi-desert. A ford takes them 2.5 game days
too. The Nomadic Host
needs twice the foot soldiers' time. A Runner takes half the foot time on land.

A fully crewed Galley sails **3 coastal hexes per game day** or **5 deep-sea hexes per
game day**, **2 river hexes per game day**, and takes **1 game day** through a ford. A War Galley
needs 60% of the Galley's time; an Emporos needs 140%. A short crew or a carried
land unit slows a marching ship. Runners aboard follow their carrier's journey.
Cargo journeys use the separate [[routes|caravan rule]]: 1.5 times the base route
time, including at sea; cargo does not change their speed.

These are base costs before rounding the whole journey to at least one game day.
The route and its costs are fixed at departure. A journey already underway keeps
its recorded costs and arrival game day when the movement rules change. A finished
[[roads|road]] shortens the hex it leads into for everyone who walks it.

An expedition preview shows its planned length. For a unit in garrison it can also show the planned homecoming **if it departed immediately**. The order may still need physical delivery. The preview names the selected first destination; its route and arrival time remain undisclosed.

A march preview applies the same expedition budget checks as the order. Before sending an expedition, both the web menu and Keryx check its duration without dispatching anything. A refused or unavailable validation sends no Runner: choose a longer duration or a nearer area. A valid expedition may still have an unavailable arrival time. Unseen routes and their travel times remain undisclosed. A Host founds with `founding settle`, not a colony march. Without confirmation, nothing is sent.

If you send a new movement order to the same unit while an earlier order Runner still waits unboarded in one of your ports, the earlier order is withdrawn in the same dispatch. That Runner walks home; the new order still travels physically. A Runner already aboard a ship or travelling elsewhere continues on its own course, and an independent stance order is unaffected. Your dispatch receipt says when it withdrew an earlier order.
A march moves selected forces along a physical route to a destination.
On a road, every hex you **enter** takes the same time **whatever the ground** — a hill or desert hex costs no more than a plain. Time per hex over a road edge:

| Traveller | Time per hex on a road |
|---|---|
| Foot soldiers | 0.75 game day |
| Runners and messengers | 0.35 game day |
| Caravans | 0.6 game day |
| Chariots | 0.4 game day |
| Ships | no effect |
(Off the road a foot soldier needs 1 game day on plains, 2 on hills and 3 in semi-desert, so a road helps most where the ground is hardest.)

Roads join **land** hexes: plains, river valley, river delta, olive groves, maquis, hills, cedar forest and semi-desert. They never cross water or mountains, and there are **no bridges** — a road ends at a river ford and the ford is waded as before.

**War → Forces → Build road** (or `keryx unit build-road --unit <id> --to q,r`) orders one army to build **one edge**, from the hex it stands on to a neighbouring hex. For a longer road, give another order.

The **stone** leaves your nearest city the moment you give the order — you are told at once if it has too little. It travels as a caravan to the first hex, and a [[runners|Runner]] carries the order to the army, which marches there. **Building starts only when both the stone and the army are at the first hex.**

| Ground the road reaches | Stone |
|---|---|
| Plains, river valley, delta | 8 |
| Olive grove, maquis | 12 |
| Hills, cedar forest | 16 |
| Semi-desert | 24 |
Three plains edges cost 24 stone. A hundred men build a plains edge in **1 game day** and a hill edge in **2**; fewer men take longer. When the edge is finished you get a **RoadEdgeBuilt** notice.

- The stone caravan is a physical caravan and **can be intercepted** ([[transfers]]). Then the road is not finished and the stone is lost.
- A **new order** to the army cancels its unfinished road. The army being destroyed or drawn into a [[battle]] before the edge is done ends it too. **Stone is never refunded.**
- A road still waiting for its stone or its army stays listed — `keryx roads` shows what each is waiting for.
You see a road edge only where your people have seen or remember **both** of its hexes. Unfinished roads of your own are drawn dotted.
Related: [[marching]], [[transfers]].
A road is a built connection between neighbouring land hexes.

<!-- src: server/internal/combat/road.go, server/internal/province/roads.go -->
A **road** is a worn way between two neighbouring hexes, built by an army out of stone. Once it stands, **everyone** who walks it travels faster — your people, your messengers, your caravans, and your enemy's. It never decays and needs no upkeep.

- **fortify** — dig in and hold this ground. The unit cannot move until the stance is cleared. Battle participation stays at 90%.
- **storm** — assault posture against an adjacent city. Halves what its wall absorbs, at the cost of much heavier losses of your own.
- **sentry** — watch this ground. The unit spots marches passing nearby and **intercepts** enemy caravans within reach. You are alerted when it catches something.

records.section: A unit already on the march
records.text: You can give a marching unit a stance too — from **War → Forces**, or by picking a stance when you right-click a new destination for it. The order goes by [[runners|Runner]], and the Runner has to **catch up** with the unit: the game tells you where and roughly when it will reach it. From then the unit carries the stance, and it takes hold **where the unit stops** — fortify digs in there, sentry watches that ground, storm goes into the assault it is marching on. A stance never turns a unit off its road.

records.section: A unit already on the march
records.text: If the unit is too far ahead for any Runner to overtake, the Runner follows it to its destination and the stance applies where it stopped.
A unit in **fortify** or **sentry** on a hex that a neighbouring city holds lets you take it by placing a citizen there — see [[catchment]]. A unit that is only passing through does not.
Forces in sentry on the hexes an enemy city works stop those hexes feeding it. Hold that long enough and the city gives up without a battle — see [[sieges]].

A unit standing in the field eats more than one in garrison, with nothing to forage ([[upkeep]]). Post watches where they buy you warning time — on the roads an enemy would take — not everywhere. See [[defence]].

From the command line there are also dedicated watch orders: a ship on **patrol** at a coastal hex, which comes home by itself when the patrol ends, and a land unit **posted** as a forward watch until you recall it ([[keryx]]).
When your men break off a battle is set in two places:

- **For the whole realm** — **War → Forces → When to retreat**, or `keryx retreat-default` ([[keryx]]). Choose **Hold to the last man** or **Retreat when it goes badly** (the default). The latter withdraws when 20% of the side’s starting strength remains. Every unit carries this into a battle it enters. It applies at once, since no one has to carry it anywhere, but only to battles entered from then on — a battle already under way keeps what its forces brought.
- **For one unit, in the battle it is fighting now** — the **this battle** selector on its card in **War → Forces** (it only appears while the unit is fighting), or `keryx unit retreat-order`. Choose the same two modes. It overrides the realm setting for that battle only. On a field unit it is an order, and travels by [[runners|Runner]].
In Keryx, use `--hold-to-last-man` or `--when-losing` with either command. Fixed loss percentages are no longer a choice.

A **stance** tells a unit how to behave where it stands. Set it in the order menu when you march, or later from **War → Forces** with the stance selector and **Set** — which, for a unit in the field, is an order carried by [[runners|Runner]].

records.section: You are told when something comes
records.text: When a foreign army is seen marching, you get a *foreign march sighted* notification. It only fires if one of your eyes sees it: a settlement, a unit, a messenger on the road ([[sight]]).

records.section: You are told when something comes
records.text: You see **which way it is going — never where**. An army walking round a mountain can look, for a while, as if it were heading somewhere else. If its heading points at the lands of one of your cities, the notice says so and tells you **when it would get there, if that is its goal**. Treat that as a warning, not a promise: it may turn. If it turns toward you later, you are warned again.

Orders are physical ([[runners]]). The attacker's army walks the whole distance to you; your answer usually has a much shorter way to go — from your city to the nearby forces, or to the garrison already there. **Distance is the defender's ally.**

- Post forces in **sentry** on the approaches — roads, river crossings, the coast ([[stances]]).
- Keep a ship at sea near your coast.
- Well-filled [[food|food stores]] buys time against a [[sieges|siege]].
- Walls absorb damage in [[battle]] ([[buildings]]).
When you come back after being away, **foreign marches are among the first things to read** ([[coming-back]]).
In a game where nobody is online all the time, defence is mostly a matter of **knowing early** — and then having time to answer.

If your forces defend a hex, or you own the city there, you receive a dispatch when battle begins: *"Idomeneus — battle has begun at Petras"*, with its clock time. It names the opposing Wanax and the place you can already see; it reveals no march route or home city. Select **Take me there** to see the hex. With sound on, you hear the same clash as for a battle's outcome.

Each defending Wanax receives one notice per battle, even with several forces. Reinforcements do not repeat it; a new defending Wanax receives a first notice when their forces join. You can mute the dispatch and still find it in **Notifications**.
A battle is not one roll. It runs over several game days, and it always resolves the same way from the moment it begins. What decides it:

- **How many of your men actually fight.** 90% of each side engages each round. This participation is fixed for every city.
- **What kind of men they are.** An ordinary soldier strikes once; Bronze Guard three times as hard; chariots five. This is what [[bronze]] buys.
- **Walls**, if a city is involved. A wall absorbs a fixed amount of damage each game day — a shield, not a sword. **storm** halves it, at a price.
- **When they break.** A side that has lost enough routs and withdraws with its survivors. Annihilation is the exception. You choose how much is "enough" for your whole realm under **War → Forces → When to retreat** — **Hold to the last man** or **Retreat when it goes badly** (the default, retreating when 20% of starting strength remains) — and can override it for one unit in the battle it is fighting; see [[stances]].

You are told the outcome, with the losses on both sides — for example *"Victory at Petras — your spearmen (100→61) vs Idomeneus's chariots (40→12). The field was taken."* You hear the clash of arms if sound is on.
Winning at a city does not make it yours. It becomes **occupied** — see [[occupation]]. A city can also be taken without any battle at all, by hunger: see [[sieges]].

**Mistress of the Walls** ([[rites]]) strengthens only the casting Wanax's own garrison defending the blessed city, for 6 game days. It gives no bonus to an attacker, a field army or a new owner of the city.
**There is no declaration of war.** If your army arrives where a hostile army is, or a unit on watch catches a march going by, a battle starts by itself.

You do not need to break a wall. Put forces in **sentry** ([[stances]]) on the hexes a city works, and those hexes stop feeding it. Hold that long enough, with the city's food need uncovered, and **it capitulates on its own** — without a battle. The wall is never breached; the belly gives up.
This is the most powerful thing in the game that needs no [[bronze]], and the reason a city that cannot feed itself from its own [[catchment]] is fragile however thick its walls are.
A hex held by a hostile watch is **blockaded**: your people standing there produce nothing for you while it lasts. You are told when a hex is blockaded and when it is freed.

Where two cities' [[catchment|catchments]] overlap, the hex belongs to the city with citizens on it. A rival with a unit of their own in [[stances|fortify or sentry]] there can take it by placing a citizen: your citizens on it go home to your idle pool, your building on it becomes theirs at the same level, and a build you had queued there is cancelled and refunded. You get a **HexTaken** notification naming who took it and how many of your citizens are idle. Take it back the same way. If your own unit is standing guard on the hex, it must be defeated first.
You get a notification when a siege begins and when it is lifted. The City drawer carries a red banner naming who holds the approaches, and the map draws a dark cloud over the city.
What helps:
If the city falls, see [[occupation]].
A siege threatens a city by holding the ground that feeds it.
Hold it unchallenged long enough and you are told the city is ripe. Then you may:
Doing nothing leaves it occupied, which is the safe and reversible choice.

Sack and burn are offered as soon as the city falls; annex only once it has stood unchallenged long
enough. Make the choice from the dispatch that told you about it — sack/burn/annex are buttons right
there, no need to leave the browser — or from the command line with `keryx occupation` ([[keryx]]).

You are notified when your city is occupied, when an occupation is broken, and — if it comes to that — when it is sacked, looted, burned or taken. A relief force is your answer: every fight at the city resets the occupier's countdown.
If the city you lose was your last, see [[last-city]].
Winning at a city — by [[battle]] or by [[sieges|siege]] — does not transfer it. It becomes **occupied**: still owned by its Wanax, garrisoned by the victor's survivors, its production frozen.

This is a deliberately contestable window. **Any new fighting resets the clock.** Both sides are told so plainly; the defender learns that the city is *not lost yet — a relief force resets the enemy's countdown.*

A ship at sea **turns home early** when its food is only enough for the voyage home, with one game day in reserve. It uses its actual crew and any carried soldiers to work out the ration. A ship heading to a city it can still reach with its food may continue there for provisions instead.

**You hear the reason when the ship reaches home**, not while it is far away: “Nike came home early — food for the way back only.” The report names the ship and its surviving crew. It does not mean that the crew starved to half strength.

## Hospitality

When a ship reaches a city, **its own or another Wanax’s**, the city gives it food for the voyage home. This applies to messenger passage, trade and freight. The port uses grain, fish, oil and wine from its stores, **after keeping enough for its own people’s daily meal**. It gives only what it can spare; an empty port cannot supply food. Hospitality takes no silver and needs no consent. The host gets no notice naming the visiting ship or its owner; the provisions appear as ordinary food use.

At sea, a ship eats the food carried aboard. See [[sea]], [[food]] and [[upkeep]].

**Field pay starts at 1 silver per 100 people per game day**, the wage of a worker. Spearmen draw **0 silver**. A full hundred-man Bronze Guard cohort draws **1.5 silver in the field and 0.75 at home**; a full chariot cohort draws **4 in the field and 2 at home**. Remaining men determine the bill, so a half-strength cohort draws half the pay.

**Home pay is always half field pay.** Garrison, repairs and fitting out count as home. Marching, posted troops, freight missions and soldiers embarked aboard a ship count as field service. Soldiers’ pay does not flow back into the city: the stated silver bill is what the city loses.

**Only War Galley rowers draw silver pay**, per surviving crew member at 1 silver per hundred in the field and half at home. A full War Galley (50 rowers) draws **0.5 silver in the field / 0.25 at home**. Galleys and Emporoi draw **0 silver**, in port and at sea, and cannot desert for lack of silver. Carried soldiers draw their own field pay in addition to their ship’s crew.

If you cannot pay, you are warned first; if it goes on, **men desert**, and a unit that loses everyone is gone. Recruit professionals only when you can keep paying them. A spearman cohort costs 12 grain and 100 people to recruit, with no silver.

An empty ship **Laid up** in its own Harbour costs **0 silver and 0 ship food**. Its crew has returned to the city’s population and eats as civilians. **Fit out** drafts that crew back immediately; home-rate ship food and, for a War Galley, half field pay resume while the ship spends three game days preparing. See [[sea]].

Soldiers use the same four [[food|food goods]] as the people. Livestock remains emergency food for civilians, not an army ration. A full spearman cohort uses **0.5 food per game day in garrison**, or **1 food in the field**. A unit in garrison eats from its city. **A unit in the field eats double**, and there is nothing to forage — so a long march, a siege line or a posted watch is a real cost ([[stances]]). <!-- src: server/internal/combat/upkeep.go upkeepFieldGrainFactor -->

**Rowers eat like soldiers.** A ship feeds its actual surviving crew: each rower uses the same food as a spearman. A full Galley (20 rowers) uses **0.10 food per game day in port** or **0.20 on a mission**; a War Galley (50) uses **0.25 / 0.50**, and an Emporos (10) **0.05 / 0.10**. Fewer surviving rowers eat less. Garrisoned ships, repairs and fitting out use the port ration. Marching, posted and freighting ships use the field ration, including a freight route's wait between legs. A laid-up hull has no ship ration because its crew has returned to the city. Ship pay follows the home and field rates above.

A unit that runs out of food **starves**: it loses men each game day, and can starve to nothing. A ship turns home when its remaining food is only enough for the way back, unless it can reach a city for provisions. Its owner hears the reason when it reaches home, not from far away; see [[ship-food-return]].

The Notifications archive marks when a city’s garrison starts losing men to hunger and when it stops. A recovery means that loss has stopped; it does not promise food for every soldier who may arrive later. Produce more food or send food by [[transfers|transfer]].
Your [[horde|Nomadic Host]]'s spearman escort draws no silver. The silver reserve you carry goes into the city when you settle; it does not limit how long the escort can travel.
Your army is only as large as your economy can feed and pay. Build [[food]] surplus before you build cohorts, and [[silver]] income before expanding your professional forces ([[units|Forces]]).
Soldiers eat **food: grain, fish, oil and wine**, shared in proportion to the stocks available. Professionals also need **silver pay** every game day.

Voluntarily demolishing a [[temples|temple]] angers its god. Your realm loses **10 kharis per temple level**, down to a **floor of 1**. This is an immediate consequence of your own demolition, separate from the daily chance of [[divine-wrath|divine punishment]]. It does not grant punishment protection.

Before you confirm, **City → Demolish** and `keryx demolish --type temple --god potnia` show the actual kharis loss, standing afterward and the ceiling before and after. Keryx asks for confirmation; non-interactive or `--json` use without `--yes` previews the consequences without demolishing. Run again with `--yes` to confirm. The result and the **god is angered** notification record what actually happened. Nothing is refunded, and only that temple's workers become idle.

Your best remaining temple determines the ceiling: no temple **40**, level 1 **50**, level 2 **75**, level 3 **100**. Another equally high temple can keep the ceiling unchanged. **Demolition costs kharis immediately; the lower ceiling takes no additional kharis.** Standing above it declines by ordinary daily cult upkeep; temple gains do not offset this decline. Once standing is at or below the ceiling, ordinary gain and upkeep apply again. The voluntary demolition loss still applies.

A temple destroyed by **plundering** creates **no demolition debt** for its owner. Its loss can lower the ceiling and remove its production. Cancelling construction is not demolition and does not incur the kharis loss.

When your standing crosses **30 downward** and the projected net is negative, a warning tells you your kharis, net per game day and how many game days it would take to reach 15 at that rate. It is sent once per downward crossing. A positive or zero net gives no warning. Further decline below 30 does not repeat it; recovery above 30 allows a new downward crossing to warn again.
The estimate assumes that net continues. Staff and feed your temples, then check **Kult** or `keryx status`. A mood change still has its own notice.

An actual loss gives your whole realm **seven game days of protection from further divine punishment**. A game day follows this world's pace; **Kult**, `keryx status` and the punishment notice show the protection's end in your local clock. Repeated processing does not extend it. At the end, the ordinary risk resumes if kharis is still below 15. The protection follows the Wanax, across their cities and temples.
If there is nothing to take, there is no punishment and no new protection. Protection does not stop cult upkeep or prevent losses from hunger, battle or weather.

Everyday prayers work at a level-1 temple. Spontaneous blessings need **60 kharis** and a maintained temple. Only a level-2 temple or higher lets kharis grow that far. Kharis retained above a lowered ceiling still counts. The ceilings remain **50 / 75 / 100** for temple levels 1 / 2 / 3. See [[kharis]] and [[rites]].

The gods may punish a realm **below 15 kharis**, with or without a [[temples|temple]]. Each game day brings a **3% chance**. At exactly 15 there is no risk. A punishment chooses one of your active cities that has something it can take.

| Mood | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Favorable** (60 and above) | The gods may bless you: a blessed harvest (a quarter more food for 25 game days, fish excepted) or unexpected recruits. |
| **Indifferent** (30 to below 60) | They have noticed you and do nothing. |
| **Suspicious** (5 to below 30) | Below 15, a 3% chance of punishment each game day, with or without a temple; recent punishment gives seven game days of protection. |
| **Wrathful** (below 5) | The same risk below 15, except during protection: chariots break, ships are lost, food rots or plague takes a garrison. |

A standing temple and at least **60 kharis** give a **15% chance of a spontaneous blessing each game day**. This is separate from a prayer: kharis is a requirement for prayers, never spent. The number is your standing, not a percentage. Protection temporarily removes punishment risk; a favorable mood without a standing temple cannot bring spontaneous blessings. These are dice rolls, not promises.

Higher kharis also brings true omens more often, from farther away and with more detail. Only the highest standing can rarely point to a concrete place for an urgent fact. Omens never reveal exact strength, future arrival times or routes, and do not reveal unknown place names.
Blessings and punishments arrive as notifications.

A new Wanax starts at **40 Kharis**, before founding. Rising again keeps your standing with the gods, with the floor as a minimum. Kharis never falls all the way to nothing. It fades from the start; founding does not pause decay.

Daily upkeep is **0.1 base + 0.2 per city beyond the first + 0.1 per 1,000 residents**. It counts all your active cities, including your capital, whether or not they have temples. Sunk, collapsed and razed cities do not count. Residents are the actual population in those cities, including people short of a whole citizen; armies and crews away from the population are not counted a second time. This is the upkeep of the cult, rather than an extra penalty that accelerates as your realm grows.
For **three cities with 2,500 residents altogether**, upkeep is **0.1 + 0.4 + 0.25 = 0.75 kharis per game day**. A realm without a city has the base cost only.

**Kult → Upkeep of the cult** and `keryx status` show the base, cities and residents separately, alongside projected temple production and net. One more fed temple worker gives **at least +1.05 kharis per game day**, and more when the cult’s reference offering of grain is scarce in the world. This describes the extra worker's yield: employing one also requires a free citizen, an available temple workplace and that temple's daily offering. A temple earns favour; it does not remove its city's cost.

Below **15 Kharis**, there is a 3% chance of punishment each game day **with or without a temple**. An actual punishment gives **seven game days of protection**. A game day follows this world's pace; Kult and `keryx status` show the protection's end in your local clock. Nothing taken means no new protection. See [[divine-wrath]]. A punishment chooses a random eligible city of yours with something it can take; it need not strike the capital.
Three things must be true, every game day:

1. **You have a temple.** Without one, kharis decays. Each temple belongs to one god, a city may hold one per god, and kharis is still one pool for the realm.
2. **People serve in it** — placed temple workers, 2 workplaces per level in each temple. Each earns 1.05 kharis per game day before the offering factor, scarcity and decay. See [[temples]].
3. **The temple is fed** — each temple's own daily reference gift of 0.25 grain, with local fish, timber or silver as substitutes of equal divine value. See [[temples]] for the selection order and planned gift.

In a small realm, a fully staffed, fed level-1 temple can earn more favour than the realm loses each game day. Compare the projected net; a larger realm may need more temples or higher levels. Larger temples can employ more devotion and raise kharis faster when staffed and fed.

**Your best temple sets your ceiling:** no temple **40**, level 1 **50**, level 2 **75**, level 3 **100**. Everyday prayers work at a level-1 temple. Spontaneous blessings need **60 kharis** and a maintained temple. Only a level-2 temple or higher lets kharis grow that far. Kharis retained above a lowered ceiling still counts.
Kharis decays every game day regardless. Additional cities and residents increase cult upkeep even when every city has a temple ([[colonies]]).
Kharis is a requirement for [[rites|prayers]], never spent. Everyday prayers answer when their requirements are met; they cost goods and waiting time.

An ongoing **blessed harvest** appears beside Food in the city drawer and in
`keryx status` and `keryx city`, with its yield bonus, affected goods and game days left.
The row disappears when the blessing ends; fish receives no harvest bonus.

The temple shows how much each good counts with the gods, before a particular god's preferences. What the world can spare can raise what devotion earns; this is the gods' reckoning, not a buying price. The ordinary daily offering and your choice of devotion remain separate from a prayer's one-time gift.

A notification marks each change between **Favorable**, **Indifferent**, **Suspicious** and **Wrathful**, with the new Kharis value and recorded game day. Check **Kult** for decay and temple support; staff and feed your [[temples]].

A lower ceiling takes no additional kharis; above it, daily cult upkeep lowers kharis and temple workers and offerings do not raise it. The confirmation shows the loss and any ceiling change. The **Kult** drawer has three tabs: **Kharis** for this realm-wide standing and

for every temple's god, city, level, workers and daily gift. Your standing is
shared; an offering still comes from the city named in its prayer row. See

Choose the god when you build. On the web, **City → Construct** lists one row per god; in Keryx, `keryx build --type temple --god potnia`. Building the same god's temple again raises that temple's level. Each prayer is said at its own god's temple ([[rites]]): Potnia's two prayers at Potnia's, Green Shoots at Velchanos's, The Thread Shows a Path at Asterion's, Favourable Passage at the Sea Daimons'. The web shows one card per temple.

Each temple level provides **2 workplaces**: level 1 holds 2, level 2 holds 4 and level 3 holds 6. A worker stands at one temple only. These people leave the idle pool, and cannot work another job at the same time. An empty temple has no devotion gain. Founding a city grants no automatic temple staffing.

Each placed temple worker earns **1.05 kharis per game day** before the offering factor, scarcity and realm decay. A fully staffed level-1 temple earns **2.1** before these adjustments. Kult shows local staffing and the projected realm net. <!-- src: server/internal/kharis/tick.go KharisPerTempleWorker -->

When a city holds several temples, they are planned in god-ID order — Asterion, Potnia, the Sea Daimons of Stillness, Velchanos — each against what the earlier ones left in the store. A temple's workers earn kharis only on game days that temple was fed. Kharis stays one pool for the whole realm. The temple uses **grain first, then fish, then timber, and silver last**. Silver is never required. Oil and wine are not used for this standing gift; [[rites|prayers]] keep their own offerings.

**Kult → Temple offerings** and `keryx status` show one row per temple with the reference, equivalent alternatives, the stock it would find after earlier temples, and the planned next gift, with a ✓ or ✗. If the city cannot fund the whole gift, nothing is taken and that temple earns no offering gain for the game day. Devotion and the daily decay still determine your net kharis change.

With full devotion and its daily gift, a level-1 temple can raise kharis in a small realm. Compare its gain with the cost of all your active cities and residents in **Kult → Upkeep of the cult** and the projected net. A temple does not cancel city costs, but it does not protect low standing from [[divine-wrath|divine wrath]]. Higher-level temples can employ more devotion and make it grow faster when staffed and fed.

Spontaneous blessings need 60 kharis and a maintained temple. Only a level-2 temple or higher lets kharis grow that far. Kharis retained above a lowered ceiling still counts. Levelling a temple further needs cedar.

**Kult → Temples** lists every standing temple in your realm, with its city, god,
level, workers and next daily offering. **Manage in City** opens that temple's
city for staffing or building. Demolition asks for confirmation and shows the
current kharis loss and new ceiling. Temples you have not built are listed last.

**Kult → Prayers** lists prayers across your cities, with the temple and city
where each can be offered. Prayers you can prepare now come first; prayers
whose temples are missing come last. Each Offer uses that row's city and stock.
Gods' waiting times still apply across your realm. **Kult → Kharis** explains your
realm's standing, daily change and current divine risk; see [[kharis]].

`keryx status` lists all your temples. `keryx rite --list` lists prayers across

A **Temple** ([[buildings]]) is how you keep the gods' favour ([[kharis]]). Every temple is dedicated to **one god**: Potnia, Velchanos, Asterion or the Sea Daimons of Stillness. A city may hold several temples, but **at most one per god**. They are named by their god: Temple of Potnia, Temple of Velchanos, and so on. Each temple needs two things from you.

Each prayer names its god, the minimum standing it needs, and its traditional offering. Press **Offer**: a row opens with a field for each good, filled with the prayer's recipe. Bring it as it stands, or change the numbers first.

**Kharis is never spent on a prayer.** Each of the five Minoan everyday prayers answers when you meet its standing requirement, have its god's temple, and can bring its offering. Waiting time, an active gift or an unused departure gift can still prevent a new prayer.

Bring the traditional recipe or a composed offering worth at least as much to that god. If you lack the traditional gift, **Compose offering** opens empty fields so you can choose other goods you hold. Choose some goods before bringing the gift. `keryx rite --list` marks this as **compose**; use `rite --offer good=amount` to choose the gift. In an interactive terminal, Keryx shows your chosen goods and exact amounts before asking **Cast?**; answering no leaves the gift untouched. A smaller gift is refused without taking goods. Bringing more does not improve the answer. For these prayers, `--offer-multiplier` is ignored; omitting a composed offering always brings the traditional recipe.

An answered prayer starts that god's waiting time across all your cities. **Kult** and `keryx rite --list` show the remaining wait, an active gift or a gift awaiting departure. Missing temples and insufficient kharis are named as separate requirements. Potnia's two prayers share her 24-game day wait. An active gift cannot be renewed before it ends. A gift awaiting departure cannot be renewed before it is used.

Older prayers outside the current Minoan catalogue retain their uncertain answer and offering multiplier. Their offering is spent even on a silent answer, but kharis is never spent. Old recorded outcomes remain as they happened.

The current Minoan prayers are **Potnia's Vision**, **Mistress of the Walls**, **Green Shoots**, **The Thread Shows a Path** and **Favourable Passage**, described below. `keryx rite --list` or **Kult → Prayers** shows the prayers your culture can offer and why one is unavailable. Current kharis is shown with a decimal; eligibility uses the exact pool value.

The answer or a refusal appears in the Kult drawer after you offer; it stays beside the prayers. An answer also arrives as a dispatch naming the god, the prayer and what was granted. When the god marks a place, **⌖ Take me there** goes to it. In Keryx it is listed by `keryx notifications`.

An ongoing **blessed harvest** appears beside Food in the city drawer and in
`keryx status` and `keryx city`, with its yield bonus, affected goods and game days left.
The row disappears when the blessing ends; fish receives no harvest bonus.

- **Potnia's Vision** — offer 10 grain + 3 silver. Potnia marks one source of copper, tin, silver or incense you neither see nor remember, and unknown ground within two hexes, as grey memory. It creates no living eyes and shows no moving activity. Potnia waits 24 game days after answering.
- **Mistress of the Walls** — offer 8 grain + 4 timber. Potnia strengthens your own garrison defending this city by a quarter for 6 game days. It helps neither an attacking army nor soldiers away from that city. It shares Vision's wait.
- **Green Shoots** — offer 15 grain + 2 silver. Velchanos raises grain, oil and wine yield by a quarter for 25 game days. Fish and the herd are unchanged. He waits 25 game days after answering.

- **The Thread Shows a Path** — offer 4 timber + 3 silver to Asterion. The next land caravan or Runner leaving this city takes a quarter less time on its outward leg. A land caravan can be intercepted only within one hex of an enemy army, instead of two. Runners remain sacred. Asterion waits 12 game days after answering.
- **Favourable Passage** — offer 6 fish + 3 silver to The Sea Daimons of Stillness. The next ship leaving this city takes a quarter less time and suffers no storm damage on its outward leg. A Runner aboard travels at that ship's actual speed. The Sea Daimons wait 12 game days after answering.
Vision, Walls and the two departure prayers require at least 5 kharis; Green Shoots requires 30. The temple's ordinary daily offering is separate.

A departure gift stays in the city where you offered until an eligible journey physically leaves. It is used once. It cannot follow the city to a new owner, change a journey already underway, or bless a return leg. **Awaiting next departure** appears beside the prayer while the gift is unused; the god's waiting time is shown separately. Other ongoing gifts show their remaining game days.

In Keryx, `rite --list` shows your prayers, their effects, offerings, active game days, pending departure gifts and waiting time. `rite --prayer <id>` chooses one. Omitting the ID uses the prayer marked as the culture's default — Mistress of the Walls for Minoans.

Bronze can weigh far more with the gods than grain. The temple shows their current reckoning: how much each good counts before a particular god's preferences. What the world can spare and what the god favours both change an offering's meaning. **Kult** and `keryx rite --list` show these values beside your prayers.

These are offering values. Wanaxes agree their own trade prices. You may compose an offering in the Offer row on the web, or in Keryx with `rite --offer good=amount,...`. Each god has a taste, and the row tells you what this god favours and roughly what it expects. The traditional recipe always suffices.

Any good may be offered. **Wine and oil** are offerings like any other — wine is also food, so do not give up what a hungry city needs. **Incense** is a valuable gift ([[incense]]). For everyday prayers it can help meet the offering requirement; excess value does not improve the answer.
A rite is a request made at the temple of its god.
A **rite** is a request to the gods. Open **Kult → Prayers**.

Each prayer is said at its own god's [[temples|temple]], so a city needs that temple standing: Potnia's Vision and Mistress of the Walls need a Temple of Potnia, Green Shoots a Temple of Velchanos, The Thread Shows a Path a Temple of Asterion, Favourable Passage a Temple of the Sea Daimons of Stillness. Level 1 is enough. Without it the prayer shows "no Temple of …".

Right-click the site, select **Found a new settlement on arrival**, name it, choose the unit, and **March →**. Or left-click empty land and press **Colonize →**. You get the same [[catchment]] forecast as when you [[founding|founded]] your first city.

**The unit is consumed.** Those men become the colony's population — a cohort of 100 founds a colony of 100, and nobody else comes with them. You cannot recall them and you cannot change your mind. To make a colony bigger, march more men there and [[units|disband]] them: they settle as citizens.

**They carry a colony purse.** The fixed purse comes from the city they leave: **30 silver for spearmen, 60 for Bronze Guard, 90 for chariots**. It becomes the colony's starting silver, independently of daily pay. A colony's spearmen draw no daily silver; professionals and ships still need pay ([[upkeep]]). Send more with a [[transfers|transfer]] when it needs it. Sent from a city with too little, they take what there is, and the order tells you how much short they are. A purse that never reaches a new colony comes back to whichever of your cities the men walk into. <!-- src: server/internal/combat/march_start.go colonistPurse -->
You are notified when the colony is founded, with how its food looks.

There is no free starter Farm. If the ground cannot feed them, you must — by [[transfers|transfer]] or a [[routes|standing order]] — until they stand on their own. A colony on a rich mineral site with no farmland is a real strategy, but only if you have already built the grain route that keeps it alive.

Every active city, including your capital, counts toward [[kharis|upkeep of the cult]], even with a temple. Daily upkeep is 0.1 base + 0.2 per city beyond the first + 0.1 per 1,000 residents across those cities. This supplies the realm's cult; it is not an accelerating expansion penalty. Sunk, collapsed and razed cities do not count. Check the realm breakdown in **Kult** or `keryx status` before expanding.

Open **War → Recruit → Abandon settlement**, choose the colony and press **Abandon**. The confirmation appears in the same row: press **Abandon** there to give it up, or **Keep settlement** to cancel. This cannot be undone. In Keryx, use `abandon --settlement <settlement-id>`.

You can abandon only an active colony you own. **Your capital cannot be abandoned.** The colony leaves your realm, its garrison is disbanded, and troops aboard ships in that garrison are disbanded too. Its people do not move to your capital. The ground becomes open for founding again, and you regain a settlement slot.
After confirmation, the colony disappears from your owned settlements. Keryx names the colony you gave up; the web map and settlement list refresh. Abandoning is a peaceful withdrawal.
Founding adds no grain to the colony's stores. Produce food or send it by [[transfers|internal transfer]]; the starting silver is only the carried purse.
Beyond your metropolis you may hold more settlements — up to **five** in all. <!-- src: server/internal/province/training.go MaxSettlementsPerWanax -->

This is the strategic shape of the whole world.

Bronze needs **copper and tin**. **Copper and tin are never found on the same landmass** — the world is made that way on purpose, every time. It is not bad luck, and no new world will fix it.

Therefore **nobody can make bronze alone.** Not the richest Wanax, not the luckiest start. Bronze — and with it Bronze Guard, chariots, war galleys and the best walls — exists only for those who cross water, or who trade with someone who has.

## Three roads

1. **Mine one half and buy the other.** The merchant's road, and the most common ([[trade]]).
2. **Sail and found a colony on the other metal's landmass.** Expensive, slow, permanent ([[sea]], [[colonies]]).
3. **Take it from someone carrying it.** A caravan of tin crossing your ground is a target ([[stances]]).

Then smelt it: a **Foundry** turns copper and tin into bronze ([[buildings]]).

## If you cannot find copper at all

Go and look — that is what the world is for. Every ship and every scout widens the map ([[sight]]). And you can ask the **oracle** ([[rites]]): it reveals a deposit somewhere you have never been. Getting there is up to you.

Megaron is being built while you play it. When something is wrong, the most useful thing you can do is tell us — from inside the game.

Open **Report (✎)** and choose:

- **Bug — something is broken**,
- **Design — this feels wrong**, or
- **Confused — I don't understand this**.

Write what happened and press **Send**. Your position on the map, the current game day and what you were looking at are attached automatically, so you do not need to describe them.

A *Confused* report is as valuable as a bug. If this Codex did not answer your question, that is worth a report too.

Before reporting, glance at [[rough-edges]] — it may already be known.

A dispatch action names the surface it opens: **Staff** a completed workplace, **Show** its city, **Review** a unit, **Reply** to a correspondent or **Manage route**. The selected city, site, unit or route is marked on that surface. Cargo already delivered leads to the destination city's goods; a cargo still travelling leads to its transit row. An old dispatch without a remaining target has no navigation button.

Honest notes on the current build, so you do not mistake a gap for your own mistake.

## Things that work, but awkwardly

- **March in the Forces tab takes typed coordinates**, not a map click. Right-clicking the map is the friendlier path — it also reaches forces already on the march ([[marching]]).

## Not in this version

**Kingdoms** — formal alliances, elected leaders, shared armies — are built but switched off, and will return once the foundations are proven. For now, diplomacy is [[messengers|letters]] and [[trade]].

Keryx is a single program; ask whoever runs your world for a copy. Then:

```
export POLEIA_SERVER=https://megaron.formatet.se
keryx login --username <your name>
keryx join
keryx status
```

`keryx actions` is the command to reach for when you are stuck: it lists what you can do right now. `keryx --help`, and `--help` after any command, explain the rest. The rules themselves are in this Codex: `keryx codex` lists the articles and `keryx codex <id>` prints one.

```
keryx status                 # your realm at a glance
keryx codex bronze           # read a Codex article
keryx notifications          # the archive — what happened while you were away
keryx notifications --all    # every kind, each event shown separately (latest 100)
keryx dispatches             # which kinds of news are pushed to you live
keryx map                    # the map around you
keryx city                   # people and placement in a city
keryx goods                  # stock and production
keryx password               # change your password
keryx occupation order ...   # sack, burn or annex an occupied city
```

`notifications --all` includes the historical kinds normally hidden or grouped in the default feed. It shows the latest 100 notifications; combine it with `--unread` for unread rows only. It does not mark anything read. Use `--kind` or `--exclude` separately to select kinds.
Orders given through Keryx obey the same rules as in the browser: they travel by [[runners|Runner]] and take game days ([[time]]).

`POLEIA_CONFIG` selects a separate configuration file. `POLEIA_SERVER` and `POLEIA_TOKEN` override connection settings. Command failures show the error and a pointer to `keryx <command> --help`. March previews call the soldiers' silver cost **Pay**.

With exactly one active world, commands select and save it automatically. To choose explicitly, run `keryx worlds` and then `keryx worlds --select <world-id>`. City rows show both the placement number and `(q,r)`; use those coordinates with `build --hex q,r`.

Use a city name or province ID either positionally or with `--province` in `city`, `placements`, `status` and `build`. For placement: `keryx place Knossos fish 13 -1` or `keryx place --province Knossos fish 13 -1`. Put flags before the good when using a negative delta. If no citizens work that good on the chosen hex, the result lists where they do work it. `founding settle --yes` skips the question. Travel estimates use game days; if an arrival cannot be calculated it is reported as unavailable.

Hex selection accepts the ordinal shown by City, with or without `#`: `build --type lumbermill --hex 6` or `--hex '#6'`. Placement can use `place fish 6 +1`, `place fish '#6' +1`, or `place --hex 6 fish +1`; `--hex q,r` also works. Put flags before the good when giving a negative delta. `staff` is for city workplaces; hex-bound buildings are worked with `place` on their hex.

Start construction with `keryx build --type harbour`. A positional argument in `build`
is the **city**, as in `keryx build Knossos --type harbour`; it is not the building type.
Use `build --list` for the catalogue or `build --queue` for queued construction.

`keryx staff olive_press` shows that named workplace's staffing. Add `+1` or `-1`
to change it; the building name is required. Use `keryx city` or `keryx roster`
to find workplaces and assignments. Hex buildings use `place`.

Send a report with `keryx report --text "what happened"`; use `--kind confused`
for a question the rules did not answer. For colony founding in scripts, add
`--yes`: `keryx unit march --unit <id> --target 5,-3 --intent colonize --name Thapsos --yes`.
Without confirmation, the non-interactive text command only shows the forecast;
JSON callers receive a refusal until they add `--yes`.
To learn what a contacted city needs or can spare, ask its Wanax with `keryx messenger` and read the reply with `keryx inbox`. See [[messengers]] and [[trade]].

Temple workers use the same citizen pool as other jobs. Use `keryx staff temple +1` to assign one, `staff temple -1` to free one (with several temples, add `--god <god>`), and `roster` to see their assignments. See [[temples]].

**Keryx** is Megaron's command-line client — the herald. It talks to the same server as the browser and can do everything a Wanax can do, including a few things the browser cannot do yet ([[rough-edges]]).
You do not need it to play. It exists for players who prefer a terminal, for automation, and for AI players.

For ordinary game accounts, your chat account is created after you own your first city. It uses your Wanax name, and stays with your game account across world reseeds. If account creation is pending, check again later.
AI playtest accounts are exempt: no community chat account is provided, and no chat password can be requested.

Click your Wanax name at the top left to open [[account|Account]]. Under **Community chat**, the ready account shows your chat ID and homeserver. Press **Get chat password** to set a new password and display it once. Each request replaces the previous chat password. Save it before closing the window; the game does not store it. The `agora_ready` notification opens this same account window, and never carries a password.
Open `agora.formatet.se`, or a Matrix app using the displayed homeserver, and sign in with your chat ID and password. Ask us to invite you to `#megaron-ooc`.

From [[keryx]], use `keryx agora` to check the account and `keryx agora password` to explicitly set and print a new chat password. No world needs to be selected. If Community chat is disabled on the server, no password button is offered.

- Be decent. No harassment, no hate, nothing illegal.
- Talk about the game, not other players' real lives.
- Don't post your real name, address, school, health or other private details. Your chat account uses your Wanax name, so other members can see which ruler you play.
- Report a message with the menu next to it in your Matrix app, or write to a moderator. Moderators can read what is reported.

The chat runs on our own hardware in Sweden and is not connected to any other Matrix server. The room is not encrypted, so don't treat it as private. Messages stay until they are deleted. There is no self-service account deletion in the game. To delete your account, write to the admin in the chat; the admin erases the game account, and its chat account is closed with it. Your Wanax name stays in other players' letters and chronicles.
For an in-game problem, use [[report]].

Community chat is outside the game, on Matrix. It is optional: questions, bug talk and alpha news. Chat messages do not reach the game world. There is no bridge to [[messengers]], no game commands in Matrix, and important game announcements stay inside the game.

**Catchment** — the land a settlement works: its own hex and the ring within two steps. See [[catchment]].

**Citizen** — one marker on the placement grid; one hundred people. See [[citizens]].

**Contact** — the permanent right to write to and trade with a city, earned by reaching it. See [[contact]].

**Emporos** — a merchant ship. See [[sea]].

**Kharis** — your realm’s standing with the gods. A new Wanax starts at 40; it fades from the start, with a daily cost that grows with your active cities and their residents. See [[kharis]].

**Kult** — the drawer for the gods and the temple.

**Metropolis** — your first city, founded from the Nomadic Host. See [[founding]].

**Nomadic Host** — the people you begin as, before you found a city. See [[horde]].

**Runner** — the person who carries your order to a unit in the field. See [[runners]].

**Sentry** — the watch stance; also how a siege is laid. See [[stances]].

**Food coverage** — how long the city’s grain, fish, oil and wine stocks last at current consumption. See [[food]].

**Standing order** — a caravan route that runs by itself. See [[routes]].

**The Thalassa** — the sea. See [[sea]].

**game day** — the world’s unit of time; the calendar names its date. See [[time]].

**Wanax** — a ruler; you. See [[welcome]].
